AQB is used for stress analysis and design of cross sections created with AQUA. The enhanced version AQBS allows the consideration of the special features of prestressed concrete and composite structures (prestressing tendons, imposed secondary stresses, creep and shrink- age). This manual is valid for both versions. The optional features which are operative only in AQBS are identified.
 The forces and the prestressing tendons can be defined directly or be imported from the database for beam, truss or cable elements. A whole series of design tasks can be carried out with the selected forces. These are:
 1. Creep and shrinkage analysis (AQBS only)
 AQBS can examine creep and shrinkage in up to 99 creep intervals. Different creep characteristics can be defined for each material, so that subsequently added cross section parts can be considered too. The internal forces due to creep are stored in the database and they are taken into account in later creep stages or stress determinations.
 2. Determination of the maximum stresses in the cross section according to the theory of elasticity.
 AQB can perform stress checks of any thick-walled or thin-walled cross section, including shear stresses and warping torsion in accordance with a great variety of codes for steel, timber, or prestressed concrete. Different stress limits can be considered for different materials in the same cross section.
 3. Determination of the required reinforcement or internal safety factor for unreinforced, re-
 inforced or prestressed concrete cross sections. AQB can design reinforced or prestressed concrete cross sections with an optimised dis- tribution of the reinforcement for axial force and biaxial bending. International codes can be taken into consideration. A shear design can be carried out following the bending design.
 4. Determination of the maximum stresses and actual stiffnesses for the defined material law.
 AQBS determines stress and strain distributions based on the material behaviour. This makes it possible to perform controls on crack width limits, reinforcement stress range, foundation pressures, and elastic-plastic design analysis. Also effective stiffnesses can be determined with that for a non-linear static calculation (plastic-plastic).

Determination of the maximum stresses and actual stiffnesses for the defined material law.. AQBS determines stress and strain distributions based on the material behaviour. This makes it possible to perform controls on crack width limits, reinforcement stress range, foundation pressures, and elastic-plastic design analysis. Also effective stiffnesses can be determined with that for a non-linear static calculation (plastic-plastic)..
 Computed stresses, reinforcement and stiffnesses can be stored back in the database, and they can both be graphically represented or be addressed by other modules.
 The functions for design and stiffness determination are also integrated into STAR2 in a sim- plified form. For this reason, tasks (3) and (4) can be also carried out directly with STAR2. This makes it possible to do a static design taking the material behaviour into account. When this procedure is used, however, only one design mode is possible for the entire structure. If columns and girders are to be designed with different parameters, one can make an iteration using the modules STAR2 and AQB by means of the command procedure PS (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’).
 The small version of AQB is included in the general SOFiSTiK-Licence. It allows for a reduced
 number of functions only. These are:
 - Generally only uniaxial bending but for circular sections along the main bending direction (piles)
 - Stress checks for all cross sections
 - Elastic-plastic analyses (STRE E) for rectangular, circular sections and structural steel shapes
 - Uniaxial reinforced concrete design for rectangles and T-beams and for circular/annular sections.

The external forces and moments are longitudinal or transverse forces referring to the elastic centre and the shear centre of the construction stage section used in the analysis.
 The elastic center is the point where an acting normal force will create only a centric strain and thus no moments.
 In special cases, one can select any other point in the cross section.
 For design purposes, the internal forces and moments are normally modified as follows.
 The longitudinal and transverse forces are converted to axial and shear forces. The torsional moment is dismantled in a Saint-Venant part and a secondary part from warping torsion.
 Within the defined support boundary, moments are smoothed under the assumption of a uni- form surface pressure (parabolic). The smoothing is done for each side of the beam, and the shear force at the end of the beam is set to zero.

Most newer design codes for structural steel and composite structures are based on a elastic- plastic or plastic-plastic design. To achieve this the sections are subdivided into four classes as follows:
 • Sections of class 1
 are suitable for plastic hinges and a non-linear analysis with distributed yield areas (Analy- sis option NSTR) and a detailed interaction of shear and normal stress.
 • Sections of class 2
 have limited deformation capacities. The analysis may be done according to linear theory but the design may be done up to ultimate plastic limits.
 • Sections of class 3
 have no allowance for yielding, i.e. the linear stresses are limited. Thus analysis and design are according linear theory.
 • Sections of class 4a
 are formal in class 4 but due to small stresses these sections may be treated as in class 3.
 • Sections of class 4b
 due to buckling of the plates, some parts of the section have to be treated as not effective for normal stress, which has to be accounted for either during the definition of the section or will be taken into account automatically within a non-linear analysis.
 The separation between the classes is rule by a width-to-thickness ratio c/t, defined in tables of the design codes. As the section class is not only depending on the stresses but also on the material strength, it is of little use to specify a single class for a complete section, and such a specification or evaluation of a section class in AQUA is not provided.
 The design in AQB reverts the viewing direction of the design to the consistent way and has considerable advantages for the checking and especially for the utilisation factors during plan- ning. AQB does not check that all sections are in class X, but it computes that the utilisation of the critical limit of c/t is less than the stress dependent required limit value. This allows also to use slender elements within a plastic design or non-linear analysis, if the stresses at these elements are sufficiently small.
 The check within AQB is done with the following possible variants:

AQB does not check that all sections are in class X, but it computes that the utilisation of the critical limit of c/t is less than the stress dependent required limit value. This allows also to use slender elements within a plastic design or non-linear analysis, if the stresses at these elements are sufficiently small.. The check within AQB is done with the following possible variants:.
 • Design for stresses only, checking the c/t ratio according to sectional class 1+2+3+4a and low utilisation of sections of class 4a (STRE E F)
 • Design for stresses for section class 3, and if the section is classified in 1 or 2 a design for sectional capacities with interactions according to Eurocode. (STRE C)
 • Non linear design with hardening effects for sections of class 1 and 2. (NSTR)
 • Design for stresses for sections of class 1-4 with a non-linear analysis, where the non effective parts of the plates in class 4 are deactivated automatically.(NSTR)
 For the design of sections of class 4 there are thus several possibilities:
 • For small stresses load cases not relevant for stability may use increased c/t-limits (EN
 1993-1-1 5.5.2 (9))
 • Defining NEFF areas in AQUA may create the effective sections directly.
 • Using automatic iterative evaluation of non effective parts with (NSTR)
 Due to the shortening of the c-values in AQUA by the NEFF definitions those sections are now classified as sections of class 1 to 3. Thus we encounter the question if those reduced effective sections may include yielding. EN 1993-1-1 describes in Chapter 6.2.1 (4) how to perform an elastic stress check based on effective sectional values. But then we have several hints:
 • Chapter 6.2.9.3 (1) requires only, that the stress should not exceed the yield stress.
 • Chapter 6.2.9.3 (2) defines a simplified check based on the interaction with the elastic sectional moduli Weƒƒ.
 • Chapter 6.2.2.4 describes how a section with a web in class 3 may be converted to class 2 with the introduction of non effective areas.

• Chapter 6.2.9.3 (2) defines a simplified check based on the interaction with the elastic sectional moduli Weƒƒ.. • Chapter 6.2.2.4 describes how a section with a web in class 3 may be converted to class 2 with the introduction of non effective areas..
 As a non-linear analysis including yield especially for the tensile parts but without hardening does not exceed the yield stress, this method is within the requirements of the first bullet. Chapter 4.6 on EN 1993-1-5 describes the simplified check according to 6.2.9.3 (2) as general rule, but it says also in chapter 4.2. (2): "‘Effective areas should be determined on the basis of the linear strain distributions with the attainment of yield strain in the mid of the compression plate."’

- The vertical axis has an upward arrow (utilisation level). Near the top, the value **1.0** is indicated by a **green dashed horizontal line**, representing the utilisation threshold (unity).

**Curve shape**
- A **green solid curve** starts at the origin region (near zero utilisation at low stresses) and increases gradually.
- As the curve approaches the vertical line at \(f_y\), it rises more steeply, reaching (or approaching) the **unity threshold** around that region.

**Step/jump at \(f_y\)**
- At the vertical line corresponding to \(f_y\), the plot shows a discontinuity or “step” in the reference utilization limits:
  - To the left of \(f_y\), the curve appears to approach the green dashed line (unity) smoothly.
  - Immediately at \(f_y\), the figure introduces a higher allowable/reference utilisation condition, suggested by two horizontal lines:
    - A **green horizontal line** at a level just above the unity dashed line.
    - An **orange/red horizontal line** at a higher level.
- The colored horizontal segments represent different design/regime constraints for **section classes** (as indicated in the surrounding text: transition between class 4 extended limit, then at yield the limit shifts to class 3, and beyond that geometric utilisation ratios apply, potentially exceeding 1.0).

**Annotation text**

- The bottom caption reads: **“Figure 2.3: Utilization level of section classes”**.

After crossing \(f_y\), the governing utilisation ratio jumps to higher geometric ratios for a different section class regime, meaning utilisation can exceed 1.0 and may require a non-linear analysis (NSTR) when non-effective parts occur.

For an effective design the ultimate bearing capacity is checked by utilisation levels of the total forces. The interaction of the individual components is given on a simplified way in the design codes and in general there are clauses to use modified schemes if appropriate. Very often some parts of the section are reserved for a certain force component. An other severe drawback is the non linearity of the interaction utilisation levels, i.e.
 the utilisation of a combined action may be lower than that of the largest component
 • with half of the ultimate loading the utilisation value may be anything below 1.0, e.g. 0.25 or 0.75 for a quadratic expression
 • Utilisations larger than 1.0 cannot be treated at all in many equations
 AQB provides thus five types of interaction, the user may select. All interaction formulas try to calculate a utilisation level which is as close as possible linear, i.e. giving an indication for the possible load factor. For an utilisation level of 1.0 the expressions are equivalent.
 •
 the utilisation of the yield stress by the elastic stresses (STRE E): This is the square root of the yield criterion of all effects according EN 1993-1-1 6.2.1 (5), Eq.6.1.
 •
 the summation of all individual utilisation levels (STRE B): This is equivalent to EN 1993-1-1 6.2.1 (7), Eq.6.2, however the contributions of trans- verse shear and torsion will be added separately and not included in the utilisation of the moments.
 the interaction according the consecutive equations of the Eurocode (STRE C): The shear force will be included in the utilisation of the moments, but the axial force and the torsion will be added separately.

 •
 an evaluation of a plastic interaction (NSTR KSV PLD): This method is not yet suitable for an iteration, but will only provide one point on the inter- action surface.

 The utilisation of the sectional class is obtained in AQB as follows: For very low stresses, the extended limit value for section class 4 is applicable, which is quite large, thus the utilisation level is low. The case of buckling will occur if an element will suffer from large forces due to small defor- mations induced by geometric non-linear effects. This will limit the ultimate load for slender structures.
 The design for stability can be done in either of two ways. The most common checks are done based on a single representative beam. The problem which persists is the determination of the buckling length. The other way is to perform a global analysis using second order theory and suitable imperfections. This is the general target of SOFiSTiK-Software. However there are two exceptions to this general concept:
 The design for axially compressed beams in accordance with DIN 18800 Part 2 / EN 1993 is also included under the stress design in AQB, since it is normally used for lateral buckling perpendicular to the plane of the structure and for single truss braces. This requires however the explicit definition of the buckling length coefficient.
 The design is performed by means of a degree of utilization of the buckling load.

 Eurocode EN 1999 uses in chapter 6.2.1 a unified design check based on admissible stresses and a national dependent combination constant C, increasing the admissible yield stress. This is comparable to a sectional check for sections of class 3 or 4 ( α = 1.0). The shape factor α, which is described with great details can be accounted for to a great extend with the plastic design forces in AQUA.

 The deformations (strain and curvature loads) will yield in a second step the forces if the struc- ture is constrained (statically indeterminate), which change the acting stress. If this effect is considerable, the user has to subdivide the total analysis in several creep intervals. If the num- ber of steps is increased the results will converge to the exact solution, however depending on the quality of the input parameters of course.
 If the characteristic of the development of stresses in time is known, it is possible to enhance the precision of this explicit integration scheme by the introduction of a relaxation coefficients. This value (0.5 to 1.0) accounts for the loss of the concrete stress in time due to the reduction of the constraining forces and must not be mixed up with the relaxation of the tendons themselves.
 For very simple cases of single sections it might be sufficient to reduce the acting force by the same factor which is given by the loss of prestress.

The image is a clean, monochrome technical diagram illustrating “Creep Intervals” (caption: **Figure 2.4: Creep Intervals**). The layout consists of two related plots: a left-hand step-load diagram over time and a right-hand strain (deformation) response diagram.

On the **left**, there is a horizontal time axis labeled **t**. A vertical axis marked **P** indicates the load magnitude. The load history is drawn as a piecewise-constant step function: starting from zero (or a baseline), the load **jumps upward** at an initial time to an intermediate level, stays constant for a period, then **jumps again** to a higher constant level, and finally **increases** once more to the top step. The stair-steps are aligned with increasing time intervals, showing multiple load stages acting sequentially.

On the **right**, a vertical axis labeled with incremental deformation symbols—**e1f, e1v, e2f, e2v, e2v?** (the labels visible include **e1f**, **e1v**, **e2f**, **e2v**, and **e2v** again near the lower part)—and a horizontal time axis (not fully labeled in this crop) display the resulting strain components for the corresponding creep intervals. The curve is drawn as a step-like increase for each interval followed by a **time-dependent (creep) evolution**. For each loading interval, two conceptual contributions are shown: a **“f” part** (plastic/yield or immediate irreversible component—drawn as a sudden step) and a **“v” part** (viscoelastic/delayed elastic component—drawn as a gradual, curved change). The diagram visually indicates that when a new load is applied, the instantaneous/irreversible part contributes as an abrupt change, while the delayed elastic part develops and is “rebuilt” with new coefficients for the new interval.

Overall, the figure communicates that creep analysis is performed across discrete time intervals: each interval’s applied load produces an immediate irreversible component and a delayed component that progresses over time. The caption and the connected mathematical context (from the provided text) suggest this relates to the decomposition of creep into a plastic yield portion plus a delayed elastic (time-delayed) portion, with the delayed part recalculated for the effective concrete age in each stage.

 The prestressing of the tendons is used with their values after creep and shrinkage taking into consideration the decompression due to the internal forces and moments on the reduced net cross section. The initial strain is determined by the actual values of the internal forces and moments, and then multiplied as a whole by the prestress factor.

The reinforcement in AQUA has been arranged in layers. The reinforcement of a layer is considered as tension reinforcement if the centre of the total reinforcement lies on the tension side relative to the centroid of the cross section. A reinforcement with its centre on the other side is regarded as compression reinforcement. The meanings of the layer types are as follows:
 M Minimum reinforcement
 The intended minimum reinforcement is defined by the basic reinforcement area. If the minimum reinforcement should be always applied and not be increased, the maximum reinforcement area must be set equal to the basic reinforcement area. If the maximum value is larger than the minimum value, the user may select for the design if the layer is always inserted with at least the defined minimum area for beams. Compressive members will always activate the minimum value, but the minimum reinforcement in the compression zone however is applied only when a corresponding tension reinforcement is also present.
 Z Supplementary reinforcement
 Layers of this type are optional. The layers are equivalent in ranking; the number serves only for identification. The value of the basic reinforcement area is only used to specify the reinforcement ratio between the individual positions, and it is not a specification of minimum reinforcement. If supplementary reinforcements are not permitted to exceed a certain value, an appropriate maximum value must be input.
 S Sequential layers
 This type of layer serves to control the sequential filling of the reinforcement layers known from older programs. When a maximum value is reached, the next higher layer number is addressed. The reinforcement of layer 0 can be defined as minimum reinforcement with layer type M; all other layers must be of type S and have no minimum reinforcement.
 Reinforcement with the same layer number is always increased by the same factor. The maxi- mum factor is given by the first element reaching the maximum reinforcement in the layer. The minimum factor is 0.0 for layers (S,Z) and 1.0 for active minimum reinforcement layers (M). Maximum values may be ignored in the determination of the minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section.
 A design must find, by iteration, a strain estate and a reinforcement distribution by which exter- nal and internal forces match. Additional requirements for ductility trigger either safety factors depending on the tensile steel strain or establish limits for the height of the compressive zone. If the height of the compressive zone exceeds the specified limits, compressive reinforcements are required. But they should not be taken larger than the tensile reinforcements.

A design must find, by iteration, a strain estate and a reinforcement distribution by which exter- nal and internal forces match. Additional requirements for ductility trigger either safety factors depending on the tensile steel strain or establish limits for the height of the compressive zone. If the height of the compressive zone exceeds the specified limits, compressive reinforcements are required. But they should not be taken larger than the tensile reinforcements..
 The class of possible strain states is further limited in such a way that only the ultimate limit strain states are used. This reduces the number of unknowns in the strain plane to two. How- ever, as additionally unknown factors of the reinforcement distribution are also present, there might be more unknowns than conditions for the solution.
 For this reason, problems with more than one reinforcement layers do not always have one unambiguous solution. Even with all the possible additional conditions (3), one can find a unique solution for a maximum of 4 to 6 layers, depending on the strain range.
 The procedure runs in two steps. The limit strain state is iterated in the outer loop by the BFGS method, similarly to what was described in the previous section.
 • As a rule, a first attempt to achieve equilibrium is made with a strain variation between the optimum tensile strain S1 to the maximum compressive strain C1 and a variation of the reinforcement distribution. If this is successful while the limiting conditions are maintained, an optimum ductile solution has been found, where the limits on the height of the compres- sive zone (x/d) are fulfilled. If this does not happen, the further procedure is determined depending on the axial force.
 In case of compressive loading, the strain on the tension side is reduced to the point where equilibrium is reached with a symmetric reinforcement distribution. The compressive zone must be enclosed with shear links.
 •
 • In case of tensile loading, the following strain variations are successively used in search of equilibrium:
 a) Centric strain S2 per thousand
 b) Compressive strain between 0 and C1 Tensile strain between S1 and S2
 c) Fully tensioned cross section with variable tensile strain
 The distribution of reinforcement is found in the inner loop by means of a quadratic optimisation problem for minimum error between internal and external forces with supplementary conditions for the required reinforcement.
 • Compression reinforcement is inserted by a magnitude not greater than the tension rein- forcement. This requirement of the old DIN is generalised by making certain that the centre of the total reinforcement is located on the tensional side of the cross section relative to its centre.

The distribution of reinforcement is found in the inner loop by means of a quadratic optimisation problem for minimum error between internal and external forces with supplementary conditions for the required reinforcement.. • Compression reinforcement is inserted by a magnitude not greater than the tension rein- forcement. This requirement of the old DIN is generalised by making certain that the centre of the total reinforcement is located on the tensional side of the cross section relative to its centre..
 • Provided that a minimum reinforcement is defined either with the section or in the data base from former design, this in this respect partial one is considered than there is not any violation of the former paragraph. To prevent increasing reinforcements for cyclic loadings, minimum reinforcement becomes always active only with its symmetric part. A special option CTRL REIN REQU may even deactivate the minimum reinforcements completely.
 Even with these limiting conditions, the problem can still be ambiguous. If, for instance, several layers could function as tension reinforcement, the distribution of the reinforcement would be based on the defined base values of the steel areas. Since this is generally not desired, the program uses additionally the distance of the reinforcement from the neutral axis and the moment of inertia with respect to the neutral axis. A supplementary condition is formulated for that purpose, which prefers reinforcement which is located farther outwards. If two layers are at the same distance, they are treated in the same manner. If the distance of a layer is zero, it is given no consideration whatsoever. Interpolation is used between these two extreme situations. Thus, a layer which is half as far out as another can only increase up to about one half the value of the outer layer.
 If the centre of some layer is at the outer extreme, only the distance of the centre is considered;
 if all of the layers have zero centre distances, only the radii of inertia (./I/A) are considered.
 This condition too is interpolated linearly between the extreme values. Furthermore, the far- ther outward the reinforcement is positioned in the cross section, the more stringent the entire condition is formulated. This supplementary condition does not affect the area of the reinforce- ment, but rather the factors of increase. Therefore, any change in the AS-values defined in AQUA will have a certain influence on the reinforcement distribution.
 The procedure of activating the layer numbers in sequence, which was customary in older programs, can not handle changing loads. In special cases, such as multilayer peripheral reinforcement or additional densifications, this method can be applied by defining sequential layer numbers in AQUA.

Therefore, any change in the AS-values defined in AQUA will have a certain influence on the reinforcement distribution.. The procedure of activating the layer numbers in sequence, which was customary in older programs, can not handle changing loads. In special cases, such as multilayer peripheral reinforcement or additional densifications, this method can be applied by defining sequential layer numbers in AQUA..
 In such case, each layer is considered individually. Layer i is laid only after layer i-1 has reached its maximum value. If a layer is not needed (e.g. compression reinforcement), it can be passed over.
 Beside the information from the cross section program on the distribution of reinforcement, there are other parameters, especially the minimum reinforcement ratios, which are controlled with the record DESI.
 The program differentiates between bending and compression members. The sequence of criteria is as follows:
 first criteria is a definition specified for the beam or design element
 •
 second criteria is the specification with the section (most common case)
 third criteria is the orientation relative to the gravity (CTRL VERT)
 •
 last criteria is the magnitude and eccentricity of the normal force (e.g. e/d<3.5)
 •
 One constructional reinforcement value can be prescribed for each type. This is an important option in stability studies. The minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section can also be considered for compression members.
 These minimum reinforcement values hold equally for all cross sections of an analysis run and they are input as percentages of the cross sectional area.
 The new reinforcement is the greatest of:
 reinforcement required by the current design
 - minimum constructional reinforcement
 - minimum reinforcement of the statically required section
 - minimum reinforcement defined in the cross section program
 - minimum reinforcement that has already been stored
 The so computed reinforcement is used in subsequent checks.

The minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section is applicable to compression members. AQB recognises a compression member either by an explicit specification through the record BEAM or by the orientation relative to the gravity direction or, depending on the load
 case, by a relative eccentricity e/d < 3.5 and the limit axial force NLIM (record CTRL).
 The minimum reinforcement according to DIN is computed by the method of first determining the internal forces and moments that can be sustained by the cross section with an appropri- ate reinforcement (e.g. 0.8 percent), and then reducing the reinforcement in proportion to its relative strength.
 The minimum reinforcement for compression members according to EN 1992, on the other hand, is accounted as follows (distinct values are defined in the national annexes):
 Asmn = mn(0.10 · N/βs,0.002 · Ac)
 (2.33)
 As minimum reinforcement is used the one layer, in case there is only one, or the minimum reinforcement layer, in case there are many, or the supplements in cases of cross sections with supplements only. Any entered maximum values of layers are ignored in this case. If multiple layers are involved, the criteria of the previous section for the selection of the layers are used. Outer reinforcement is thus given preference.
 When the relative strength has been obtained, each layer is reduced by the same isotropic factor. If the minimum reinforcement were attained exclusively by means of a layer laying on one side only, at reduction by this method the minimum reinforcement ratio is not reached under circumstances. An alternative method which admits priority to the absolute steel area can lead to serious underdesign and is therefore unavailable.
 Clearly comprehensible results are obtained when only one layer with minimum reinforcement = maximum reinforcement is defined, with usable distribution and relatively small total quantity of steel, and all supplements lie on separate layers. The program changes then the minimum reinforcement onto the necessary value.

The truss analogy of the shear design requires a tensile force in the longitudinal direction!
 An optimal solution would introduce this force just from the beginning in the bending design, as the accounting of the compressive forces afterward is rather difficult. This design method is given in the Eurocode for the case of the transverse shear and may be selected in AQB with input CTRL VM.
 A drawback however is that the inclination of the struts has to be selected in advance or by iteration and that point loads may lead to excessive values of the reinforcements if the shear force changes the sign.
 But as there is no need to design for more reinforcements than required at the location of the maximum moment, it is quite common for best practice to use a shift rule with an offset for the required reinforcements. Then we get additional reinforcements on both sides for a zero moment which is a clear hint, that the longitudinal force is to be applied on the total section.
 For the torsional problem the standard workflow is to evaluate the utilisation of the provided total reinforcment for bending and to add the required torsional reinforcements. The true amount is only known if the inclination of the truss model has been selected. A required longitudinal
 reinforcement of 50 mm² for an inclination of 45° will yield for a cot of 1.75 thus a required longitudinal reinforcement of 875 mm² for Torsion. If then an existing reinforcement of 1000 mm² has a relative capacity of 2.5, the required reinforcement will be 1000/2.5 + 875 = 1275 mm². This reinforcement may be adopted to compressive forces within the section, which is not an easy task, but AQB will try to do so.
 As in many cases the torsional design uses an inclination of 45°, it is easier and much more economique, sometimes for existing structure possibly the only solution to go with an additional tensile force to the design similar to the transverse shear design.

 If nothing else is defined AQB will just check the strain and print an error message if its value exceeds the limit of the stress-strain-law.
 •

The design is also suitable for unreinforced cross sections. In such case the program computes internal forces and moments which are in the same proportion to each other as the external forces and moments. The safety factors must be defined according to the particular code. The program then reports the relative strength and prints a warning if this becomes less than 1.0. A message is also printed when the strain at the gravity centre becomes positive, meaning that a gaping joint is extending beyond the centre.

(the sectional values will be kept unchanged for this estimate)

This is used for all elastic stress checks, but it can be taken as a fallback or lower limit for the other methods if the values are reduced by a factor obtained from the internal lever in cracked condition to the uncracked condition.
 • The method of differences of longitudinal forces is mainly used for flanges and bond in composite sections (dowels)
 • The variable angle strut model is used for cracked conditions. It is the base for most design codes for uniaxial shear.
 The shear design for ultimate limit states is always defined as the resultant magnitude of the shear stress along the width b0. Thus we consider a shear flow T in [kN/m]. The torsional shear based on an equivalent hollow section Mt/2Ak may be added then easily. As a shear or principal compressive stress is valuable for the engineer we use and show these values too. The utilisation ratio for a total design force is not useful in general cases.
 No reduction is made of individual loads in proximity to the support. A consistent solution is extremely elaborate. Thus, only the reduction caused by the distributed pressure of the support is accounted for.

sections: 2.7.4 Shear Checks in Circular Cross Sections

content:
In case of circular cross sections AQB uses as width according to a paper by Feltham a value derived from the area above the resulting shear force and the effective height.
 Design is always done for the uniaxial resulting components of the forces or moments.
 The inclination of the shear links will be accounted for according to Bender [2].

content:
The determination of a stress state while accounting for the material properties is the basis for many further checks. For this purpose, one must follow the procedure described in Section 2.4 to determine the strain under service loads or increased service loads. No strain limits nor safety coefficients are in effect for this check. The user can apply a modified material law for this check.
 In general, this task can only be solved iteratively. To accomplish this, the strain level of the cross section, which is defined by the strain in the centroid and the curvatures in the two coordinate directions, must be varied until the internal forces and moments of the cross section sufficiently match the external ones.
 The so-called BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) method is used for the non-linear iteration. From the differences between internal and external forces a direction of change is computed for the strain level, and iteration proceeds in this direction until it reaches an optimum point. This procedure is called line-search, and its precision can be controlled by some input for the CTRL record. Starting from the calculated optimum point, a new direction is determined in the next step of iteration, using all the information computed thus far.
 The mathematical prerequisite of convexity means, from mechanical perspective, that if the curvature increases the internal moment must increase too. If stress-strain curves with falling branches are defined, the solution can become ambiguous and the procedure may run into difficulties.
 Either the serviceability stress-strain curves or the ultimate stress-strain curves or an impute mean value stress-strain curve with or without safety coefficients defined in AQUA may be applied. As the choice of the correct curve may have considerable effect on the results, each user should carefully select the best curve along his knowledge or opinion. As a guide-line the EC2 states the following rules:
 • The evaluation of deformations and the distribution of forces should use the mean values (Ecm, fctm) in general. (A 2.1 (3))

As the choice of the correct curve may have considerable effect on the results, each user should carefully select the best curve along his knowledge or opinion. As a guide-line the EC2 states the following rules:. • The evaluation of deformations and the distribution of forces should use the mean values (Ecm, fctm) in general. (A 2.1 (3)).
 • For bracing elements, i.e. those where a lower stiffness is unfavourable, the mean values of the concrete have to be divided by a safety factor of the material. (A3.4 (6) und A3.1 (6)). As these factors do not coincide with those of the design itself, they have to be specified with the stress-strain law within AQUA.
 • For the evaluation of the ultimate limit state one has to use design values. (A 2.1 (4)).
 • For the design with the total system, reduced safety factors for the loading as well as for the concrete may be used. (A 3.1)
 The design takes into account any reinforcement possibly computed for the stored load cases. If no reinforcement has been computed, or if a single combination of forces and moments has been defined externally, the program uses the minimum reinforcement ratios set in AQUA.

A special case of non linear behaviour is the effect of local buckling as it is defined in Eurocode EN 1993-1-5.  The serviceability check uses a given interpolation factor between tables 7/8 and 9/10. Table 9 and 10 have been extended for smaller stresses according to the theoretical base.
 The B 4750 has additional factors for the creep coefficients if the strength is higher than 35 MPa. The deductional areas of tendons is always the full duct area.

The mean value of permissible inclination for shear force and torsion is freely selectable be- tween 25 and 45 degrees within SIA 262, the maximum allowed shear is given by equation (40):

Shear design according to BAEL-91 as modified in the year 1999 still uses the deductional stress method. The admissible stresses depend on the inclination of the shear links (A5.1,21), but have the same value for all type of shear. There is a factor k which modifies the shear force of the concrete depending on the normal force and bending stresses. (A5.1,23).
 The design for cracking is done via a limit for the stresses according to A.4.5,323.

The ministerial decret from 1996 allows the design according to the EC with the Italian material definitions. But there still exists the old method with a deductional stress. A special option is the parameter δ, which has a value between 0 and 2 depending on the normal force and the decompression moment. This value is then applied as a factor to the shear force of the concrete. Further it has to be noted that the admissible shear stress is depending on the inclination of the shear links. This document contains also a regulation for the use of the old EC2 with the formulas of the eurocode and the materials of the DM-1996. (Safety factor of concrete is 1.6, Inclination of struts in truss model is 0.5 < tan < 1.0 etc.).
 NTC (Norme Tecniche) of year 2005 was an intermediate solution, where material safety (1.9/1.5) was referred on the cubical strength Rck of the concrete. The crack width accord- ing Table 5.1-X is also depended on the sensitivity of the reinforcement, and the stresses had to be checked for the serviceability condition according to table 5.1-XI and 5.1-XII depending on the environmental conditions.
 The NTC (Norme Tecniche) of year 2008 is now nearly identical to the EN 1992 fast vollständig überein. Small deviations are in the material parameters only. ## Overall record/block semantics (context)
Input is organized into **blocks**. Each block ends with the record **`END`**. Within a block, the user may select any **load case** and **beam combination**, which the program then processes using the specified design operations. The program stops when it encounters an **empty block** (`END/END`). The records **`HEAD`**, **`END`**, and **`PAGE`** are referenced as general documentation items from the manual “SOFiSTiK: FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”.

## Record-by-record field description

### 1) `ECHO`
Controls output echoing/printing behavior. It contains:
- `OPT` and `VAL`: a basic option switch and its value.
- `SEL E`: a further selection or sub-option indicator (`SEE LE` as shown in the table).
This record typically affects how the program echoes input or results for debugging or verification.

### 2) `CTRL`
Defines control parameters. It contains:
- `OPT` / `VAL`: option-value pair.
- `VAL2`: a secondary parameter value.
Used to adjust runtime behavior such as solver/design settings or execution control.

### 3) `BEAM`
Selects or defines a beam segment/parameterized region or sweep. Its items are distributed across multiple lines and include:
- Range/step controls: `FROM`, `TO`, `STEP`
- Classification/type: `TYPE`, `BETA`, `BETS`, `STYP`, `STYP`, `PRED`
- Axes/coordinates: `X`, `Y`, `Z`, including derivatives/variants like `XX`, `ZZ`, `AZ`, `AR`, `UZ`
- Lamella/thickness-like parameters: `LAMS`, `LAMT`, `LAM L`, `LAMC`
- Coordinate system or constraints: `CS`, `CS0`, `CS1`, `CS2`, `CS3`, `CS31`
- Similar numeric controls: `NO`, `NOB`, `MNO`, `ICS1/ICS2/ICS3`, `X/Y/ Z` variants, `DZ`, `NY/NZ`, `TEMP`
- Many parameters come in structured sets, indicating the record can specify different regimes (e.g., coordinate-based evaluation vs. sectional indexing).

In practice, `BEAM` acts as the main geometry/element selection driver, letting the user target specific beam regions or analysis points.

### 4) `END`
Terminates the current record block. Items listed include:
- `NO`, `NOB`, `MNO`: termination or option indices.
- `TYPE` / `CST` / `REF` / `TITL`: metadata for the end/summary behavior (type/category, cost/constraint setting, reference id, title).
- `LC` context selection: `LC` record name is shown separately but `END` fields suggest it interacts with load-case context (`GAMU`, `GAME`, `PSI0..PSI2`, `PS1S`, `GAMA`, etc.).
- The table shows multiple parameter groups: `GAMU/GAME`, `APAR/SUP/FAT`, and also `S`/`COMB`-related fields below, indicating `END` participates in concluding stored parameters for the processing step.

### 5) `LC`
Specifies a **load case selection** and its parameters:
- `NO`: load case number.
- `TYPE`: load case type.
- `CST`, `REF`, `TITL`: case coefficients/settings, reference identification, and title/label.
- Additional parameter sets: `GAMU`, `GAME`, `APAR`, `SUP`, `PSI0`, `PSI1`, `PSI2`, `PS1S`, and `FAT`.
This record configures how a particular load case is interpreted (e.g., gamma factors, ψ-factors, combination factors).

### 6) `S`
Appears as a sub-block/sectional option within the same overall table, with items:
- `NCS`: number of something (likely number of load/case subcomponents or cross-section settings).
- `NO`, `X`, `N`, `YV`, `VZ`, `MT`: coordinate/limit and output selection.
- `MY`, `MZ`, `MB`, `MT2`, `Y`, `Z`, `REF`: moment-related or result-selection parameters.
This suggests the record can define **sections/locations** and what quantities (moments, utilization, etc.) are relevant.

### 7) `COMB`
Defines load **combinations**:
- `EXTR`, `SCOM`: combination extraction/scalar combination controls.
- `SFAC`: scale factors.
- `LC1..LC6` and `F1..F6`: references to up to six load cases with corresponding factors.
- Alternatively named fields: `LC3`, `F3`, `LC4`, `F4`, `LC5`, `F5`, `LC6`, `F6`.

 Explanations of the CTRL-options

This table defines how bending is treated for a cross-section, depending on whether the principal axes rotation is permitted or suppressed. It provides the resulting bending model/assumptions for three output settings/columns: **MSEL (overall design option)**, **NSTR (uniaxial bending assumption)**, and **DESI (design-related uniaxial bending assumption)**. A key driver is whether the cross-section is flagged with **FSYM NO (default)** or **FSYM YES (rotation of principal axes suppressed)**.

### Row meaning: FSYM NO (default)
- Condition: **cross-section with FSYM NO (default in AQUA)**.
- Interpretation: rotation of principal axes is allowed; therefore bending is treated as **biaxial bending**.
- Resulting behavior across the table:
  - **MSEL column:** *biaxial bending*
  - **NSTR column:** *biaxial bending*
  - **DESI column:** *biaxial bending*
This means that for FSYM NO, none of the settings restrict the analysis/design to uniaxial behavior—moments may act in more than one direction consistent with biaxial bending.

### Row meaning: FSYM YES (principal axes suppressed)
- Condition: **cross-sections with FSYM YES** (rotation of principal axes suppressed).
- Interpretation: principal axes rotation is not considered, so the bending model collapses to **uniaxial bending** in combination with the moment components.
- Resulting behavior:
  - **MSEL column:** *biaxial bending* (the overall MSEL classification remains biaxial in this table)
  - **NSTR column:** *uniaxial bending* with a specific restriction: **(Mz = Vy = 0)**¹
  - **DESI column:** *uniaxial bending* with the same restriction: **(Mz = Vy = 0)**¹

¹ The footnote in the provided context clarifies the meaning of this restriction:
- **Uniaxial bending** is defined such that only one bending component is active; specifically, **Mz = Vy = 0**, and in the uniaxial-bending case the modeling corresponds to: *uniaxial bending (Mz = Vy = 0), no rotation of principal axes (yz = 0).*  
This ensures moments are not transferred into the other bending direction by rotation of the principal axes.

### Overall implication
The table essentially maps a cross-section’s **FSYM** setting to the bending behavior used for **NSTR** and **DESI**:
- **FSYM NO → biaxial bending** for all three model outputs (MSEL/NSTR/DESI).
- **FSYM YES → uniaxial bending** for **NSTR and DESI**, enforcing **Mz = Vy = 0**, i.e., suppression of principal axes rotation leads to constrained bending representation.

This mapping is likely intended to control how SOFiMSHA/AQUA interprets moment components when principal axis rotation is either permitted or explicitly suppressed.

The input table defines a configuration selector for the treatment of bending actions and the corresponding design assumptions applied to different cross-sections. It contains a header row with three key mode options: **STRE**, **NSTR**, and **DESI**. The leftmost label indicates the scope: **“all cross-sections”** are included by default.

### STRE (biaxial bending)
- **STRE** specifies that cross-sections are treated under **biaxial bending**.
- This implies that bending effects in more than one direction (i.e., in two axes) are considered simultaneously, reflecting a more general bending state than uniaxial-only assumptions.
- Under this option, the principal-axis restriction is not applied as in the uniaxial case; therefore, the model supports a full bending representation consistent with biaxial behavior.

### NSTR (uniaxial bending with principal axes rotation suppressed)
- **NSTR** corresponds to **uniaxial bending** with the condition that **\( M_z = V_y = 0 \)**.
- The table text indicates this is paired with **“no rotation of principal axes”** (conceptually: principal-axis rotation is suppressed/disabled for the affected cross-sections).
- The table footnote context states that cross-sections where rotation of principal axes is suppressed are designed with **NSTR and DESI only for uniaxial bending**, meaning these options are only valid/consistent for that simplified bending model.

### DESI (uniaxial bending with same uniaxial constraints)
- **DESI** is also configured as **uniaxial bending**, likewise under the restriction **\( M_z = V_y = 0 \)**.
- It is presented as an alternative label/selector to **NSTR**, but the table indicates both modes enforce the same uniaxial bending assumptions.
- The context further clarifies AXIA semantics:
  - **AXIA +1**: uniaxial bending  
  - **AXIA -1**: suppress rotation of principal axes  
  - and that with suppression, **NSTR/DESI are restricted to uniaxial bending only**, reinforcing that DESI participates in the “no principal-axis rotation” simplification.

### Relationship between the options
Across all listed cross-sections, the table acts as a **mode switch**:
- Choose **STRE** for **biaxial bending** (more comprehensive bending representation).
- Choose **NSTR** or **DESI** for **uniaxial bending** under the explicit constraint **\( M_z = V_y = 0 \)** and with the principal-axis rotation suppression concept tied to these uniaxial modes.

This makes the table essential for determining whether reinforcement/design checks must reflect a biaxial bending state or a reduced uniaxial bending state.

The input table is a compact reference describing the fields used to define and manage “TVAR” (nationally adjustable) variables in the software workflow. It is intended to document the standardized parameters that appear when specifying boxed values (national factors) for Eurocodes. These variables can be defined in the INI configuration files, but may also be overridden or temporarily adjusted via the `TVAR` command, including in AQB for special cases.

### Table structure and columns
The table has the columns:

- **Item**: Indicates the type of entry/field being defined.
- **Description**: Explains what that field means and how it is used.
- **Unit**: Provides any unit information relevant to the field (where applicable).
- **Default**: Shows the default indicator/value for that field.

### Rows (fields)
1. **NAME**
   - **Meaning**: “Name of a variable.”
   - **Unit**: Not applicable (left as a placeholder/implicit none).
   - **Default**: Shown as `Lit16` with a note marker `!`, suggesting an implementation-defined default behavior or a required substitution/validation rule.  
   - **Purpose**: The identifier for the boxed/national factor, e.g., names like `ALF-CE` or `GAM-CE` in the given context.

2. **VAL**
   - **Meaning**: “Value of the variable or expression in the format `”=expression”`.”
   - **Interpretation**: The user may provide either a numeric value or an expression string, enabling parametric definitions.
   - **Unit**: Not explicitly defined; depends on the specific variable being set.
   - **Default**: Shown as `Lit64` with `!`, again implying required/conditional defaults based on variable type.

3. **SCOP**
   - **Meaning**: “Scope of variable.”
   - **Role in the workflow**: Determines where the variable applies (e.g., ensuring variables are applied under the correct analysis/design scope). In the provided context, it is emphasized that for AQB input, **SCOP must be set explicitly to `DESI`**.
   - **Unit**: — (none).
   - **Default**: An asterisk `*`, indicating that there is a default scope behavior unless overridden.

4. **CMNT**
   - **Meaning**: “Comment to the variable.”
   - **Role**: Documentation/annotation for the variable definition; does not affect calculations but helps traceability.
   - **Unit**: — (none).
   - **Default**: `-` (no default comment).

### Overall purpose (as implied by surrounding text)
This table provides the schema for how `TVAR` definitions should be structured so that national Eurocode factors are correctly recognized, validated, and applied. The accompanying text highlights examples of adjusting elasticity-related parameters by setting:
- `ALF-CE` to `0.85`
- `GAM-CE` to `1.25`
with `SCOP DESI`, demonstrating that **SCOP governs applicability** and must match the intended analysis scope.

The table lists frequently used **boxed-value parameters** for **Eurocode Nationally Determined Parameters**, specifically as variable names and default numeric values that may be overridden in the software using the **TVAR** command. These factors correspond to design-scope settings under **SCOP = DESI** and relate to safety coefficients (partial factors) and long-term strength reduction factors (creep/shrinkage-related reductions reflected in EN 1992 provisions).

**Structure (columns):**
1. **NAME**: Identifier of the parameter that can be set via TVAR (e.g., `TVAR NAME "GAM-C" ...`).
2. **VALUE**: Typical/default numeric value provided for DESI usage.
3. **Comment**: Brief meaning and the Eurocode topic the factor modifies.

**Parameters for safety coefficients (GAM-*):**
- **GAM-C (1.50)**: Safety coefficient for **concrete**.
- **GAM-CE (1.20)**: Safety coefficient for **concrete elasticity** (i.e., for modulus/elastic properties rather than strength).
- **GAM-B (1.15)**: Safety coefficient for **reinforcing steel**.
- **GAM-Y (1.15)**: Safety coefficient for **prestressing steel**.
- **GAM-S (1.10)**: Safety coefficient for **structural steel**.
- **GAM-A (1.30)**: Safety coefficient for **structural aluminum**.

These GAM values act as partial factors in design verification and are central to the reliability differentiation between material types. The presence of both material-strength factors (e.g., GAM-C) and property/elasticity-specific factors (e.g., GAM-CE) indicates the model distinguishes between strength and stiffness-related design effects.

**Parameters for long-term strength reduction (ALF-*):**
- **ALF-CC (1.00)**: Long-term reduction factor for **concrete compressive strength** (EN 1992, clause **3.1.6(1)**).
- **ALF-CT (1.00)**: Long-term reduction factor for **concrete tensile strength** (EN 1992, clause **3.1.6(2)**).
- **ALF-LCC (0.85)**: Long-term reduction factor for **lightweight concrete compressive strength** (EN 1992, clause **11.3.5(1)**).
- **ALF-LCT (0.85)**: Long-term reduction factor for **lightweight concrete tensile strength** (EN 1992, clause **11.3.5(2)**).

Values of **1.00** imply no reduction (baseline case), while **0.85** represents a more conservative long-term reduction for lightweight concrete strength. These ALF parameters are intended to modify material strength values under long-term effects consistent with the referenced EN clauses.

**Contextual usage relevance:**
The surrounding text explains that Eurocodes allow national or project-specific deviations via “boxed values,” typically defined in **master.ini**, but possibly adjusted in **AQUA** using **TVAR**. For AQB special cases, the table’s parameters are examples of what can be changed temporarily—provided **SCOP is explicitly set to DESI** to ensure the factors apply to the intended design scope.

The table is a reference list of **AQUA/Eurocode “boxed values”** that can be set via the **`TVAR` command** for the **DESI scope**. These values correspond to national choices or adjustable parameters defined in INI files, and the table provides the **accepted variable names**, their **default numeric values**, and the **engineering meaning** (with relevant EN 1992-1-1 clause references where given). The table also notes that **only some of these parameters can be adjusted in AQB**, but the names shown here are the commonly used ones.

**Column structure:**
1. **NAME**: the string identifier used in the `TVAR NAME "<...>"` syntax.
2. **VALUE**: the default factor/parameter value associated with that name.
3. **Comment**: a short description of what the parameter controls, including formulas/criteria context (e.g., reinforcement ratios, strut inclination limits, or stress–strain curve modification) and sometimes the exact Eurocode clause.

**Rows / parameters included:**

- **`ALF-CE` = 0.85**  
  Comment: factor for **reducing the elasticity modulus** used for the **calculatory stress–strain curve**. This parameter directly modifies stiffness assumptions for the concrete stress–strain model (as indicated by the context text mentioning modulus reduction for the CALC curve).

- **Reinforcement ratio limits (all relate to EN 1992-1-1 design rules):**
  - **`AS-MAX` = 8.00**  
    Maximum ratio of **longitudinal reinforcement** based on **Ac** (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2(3)).
  - **`AS-MINB` = 0.13**  
    Minimum longitudinal reinforcement ratio for **bending members** based on **Ac** (EN 1992-1-1 9.2.1.1(1)).
  - **`AS-MINC` = 0.20**  
    Minimum longitudinal reinforcement ratio for **compressive members** based on **Ac** (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2(2a)).
  - **`AS-COMP` = 0.10**  
    Minimum reinforcement ratio in **compressive members** based on **normal force** (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2(2b)).
  
  - **`AS-MIN` = (not shown)**  
    The table specifically lists **AS-MAX, AS-MINB, AS-MINC, AS-COMP**, indicating these are the commonly referenced bounding ratios rather than a complete set.

- **Compressive strut inclination limits (web, compressive/compressive flanges, tensile flanges):**
  - **`TANMIN` = 0.40**: minimum inclination of **compressive struts in the web** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.3(2)).
  - **`TANMAX` = 1.00**: maximum inclination of **compressive struts in the web** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.3(2)).
  - **`TANMINC` = 0.50**: minimum inclination of compressive struts in **compressive flanges** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4(4)).
  - **`TANMAXC` = 1.00**: maximum inclination of compressive struts in **compressive flanges** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4(4)).
  - **`TANMINT` = 0.80**: minimum inclination of compressive struts in **tensile flanges** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4(4)).
  - **`TANMAXT` = 1.00**: maximum inclination of compressive struts in **tensile flanges** (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4(4)).

**Overall interpretation:**  
This table functions as a “quick reference” mapping from **TVAR parameter names** to their **numerical defaults** and **Eurocode rule targets**. It supports configuring the DESI scope so that design checks (stress–strain model parameters, reinforcement ratio constraints, and strut inclination limits for truss models) reflect selected national annex factors or special adjustment cases.

In order to be able to use the extensive possibilities for forming combinations, of creep stages and of shear designs, it is possible to define an external static system which is defined and managed independently of the existing system.

 Since tendons and internal forces and moments are also stored under the defined beam type in the database, both the load cases and the tendons must be entered after the beam sections.

For the description of construction stages the user has to select an arbitrary but unique num- bering scheme. Each change of the section, installation or grouting of tendons should have its own number. The recommended scheme is to use numbers 10,20 etc. for constructional phases, while 11,21 are used for post stressing and 15,25 for the grouting process. With AQBS every beam or beam section can be assigned up to 31 different cross sections for determining stress (e.g. gross, net, ideal). These are designated as gross and construction stage sections CS0 to CS31.

The table defines the input parameters of the **TENDON** record used to describe one prestressing tendon associated with a beam and its cross-section. It is organized as a list of “Item” identifiers, each mapping to a semantic field name, a description, its **Unit**, and a **Default** value. The record is keyed by the beam and tendon indices and contains both geometric positioning (along the beam and within the section) and behavioral parameters for tensioning, bonding stages, and crack width checks.

**Key identification fields**
- **NO (Beam number)**: selects the beam to which the tendon belongs. Unit: “–”, Default: **1**.
- **NOB (Tendon number)**: identifies the tendon within that beam. Unit: “–”, Default: **1**.
- **MNO (Material number of tendon + deduction material index)**: refers to the tendon material definition and a deduction material qualifier. Unit: “–”, Default: **1**.

**Prestressing construction stage fields (phasing)**
- **ICS1 (Prestress stage building-in)**: stage index when the tendon is installed/build-in. Unit: “–”, Default: **0**.
- **ICS2 (Prestress stage extrusion)**: stage index when post-tension extrusion (bond activation) occurs. Unit: “–”, Default: **1**.
- **ICS3 (Prestress stage removal)**: stage index for tendon removal. Unit: “–”, Default: **0**.  
Context notes: stress phases correspond to time stages; recommended values depend on bond type (e.g., immediate bond uses **ICS2 = 0**; without bond uses **ICS2 = NONE or 9999**; for delayed extrusion, **ICS2 > ICS1** is strongly suggested). Certain special external-section cases require careful ICS2 handling, including defining external tendons without bond with **ICS2 = 9999** to exclude them from crack/shear checks.

**Geometry and placement**
- **X (x value on beam axis)**: tendon coordinate along the beam axis. Unit shown as **m**, Default: **0**. Context notes: for the tendon definition mechanism, **x precision must be 1 mm**.
- **Y, Z (y/z values in the section coordinate system)**: tendon coordinates in the cross-section’s local axes. Unit: marked as “*” (value unit depends on configuration), Defaults: **0** for both.
- **YHR, ZHR (duct centre point coordinates)**: coordinates of the duct center point. Unit marked as “*”, defaults: **Y** and **Z** respectively (i.e., by default duct center coincides with tendon position).
- **NY, NZ (gradient of tendon in y/z directions)**: describes the tendon curvature/slope in section coordinates as gradients \(dY/dX\) and \(dZ/dX\). Unit: “–”, Default: **0**.

**Loads and areas**
- **ZZ (Tension force)**: tendon force magnitude. Unit: **kN**, Default: **0**.
- **AZ (Area of tendon)**: tendon steel area used in calculations. Unit: **mm²**, Default: **0**.
- **AHR (Area of duct)**: duct cross-sectional area for relevant checks. Unit: **mm²**, Default: **AZ**.
- **DZ (Effective diameter)**: effective tendon/duct diameter used for related geometry checks. Unit: **mm**, Default: “*” (preset behavior noted in context).

**Crack width reference for design**
- **AR (Reference area for design of crack width)**: governs whether and how crack width is calculated. Unit: **m²** (as listed), Default: “–”. Context notes explain that positive AR triggers an additional crack-width calculation for the tendon; negative AR can restrict crack-width calculation to reporting purposes, and a large negative AR disables crack-width design for that tendon.
- **UZ (Circumference of tendon for crack width)**: circumference used in crack width formula. Unit: **mm**, Default: “*” (preset). Context includes a formula reference using literal **BUND**: \(U = 16 - n - VAZ\) (3.1).

**Thermal loading for “hot design”**
- **TEMP (Temperature for a hot design)**: temperature parameter for designs involving thermal effects. Unit: **degC**, Default: **0**.

Overall, the record combines: (1) identification (beam/tendon/material), (2) time-stage behavior for prestressing effects via **ICS1–ICS3**, (3) spatial definition via **X, Y, Z** (plus duct centre **YHR/ZHR** and gradients **NY/NZ**), (4) mechanical quantities via **ZZ, AZ, DZ, AHR**, (5) crack-width-related parameters via **AR and UZ**, and (6) an optional thermal parameter **TEMP** for hot design.

See also: BEAM, LC
 TEND

 Tendons are generally defined with the program TENDON. For special cases and especially external sections, however, they can also be specified directly. The tendons need to be entered in order by beams and beam sections. The x values need to be specified with a precision of 1 mm. A use of this feature combined with forces directly defined with record S in load case 0 is not possible. (See example aqb2_3_t-beam-bridgesection.dat and aqb2_4_precastbeam.dat)
 The stress phases are the numbers of time stages in the progress of a construction stage, and are assigned to individual sections during the CS inputs of the BEAM record. For tendons with immediate bond, the correct specification is ICS2 0. For tendond without bond, the correct specification is ICS2 NONE or ICS2 9999, For post tensioning i.e. tendons with a delayed extrusion it is strongly suggested to specify ICS2 > ICS1.
 If a load case of TYPE PR is given an adjusting factor in a combination, then the tension forces are also multiplied by this factor.
 For the shear check it is necessary that the tendons lie within the cross section. Otherwise the proportional tensile force is computed wrongly. It is not therefore possible to combine all tendons into one single one which lies then outside of the cross section. AQB checks the situation of the tendon with a tolerance which corresponds to the radius of the prestressed steel area. External tendons without bond that are supposed to be excluded from this examination must be defined with ICS2 9999.
 The values DZ and UZ are preset to the corresponding values of an individual beam. For UZ, the literal BUND can be used to call the formula

AR can be input as a negative value, if only the amount to be calculated is desired. If individual tendons are not to be calculated in or designed at all for the crack width, then AR should be defined with a large negative value.

 Older versions of AQB used only m as basic unit for this record. This has been changed from Version 12.47 to the more common unit mm (or others selected via PAGE UNII) as within TENDON. Old definitions will be flagged with an error 13 or 14.

The table defines the schema of a “load case” record used by the AQB/AQUA design environment to drive selection of load cases, classification into design combinations, and the reference framework for stress calculation. Each row describes an input item, its meaning, expected unit/type, and a default behavior.

**1) Core identification and selection**
- **NO (Number of the load case)**: Integer identifier for the load case. It is used as the key to store and later retrieve results. Type: “-/LIT”, default “-” (no intrinsic value).
- **TYPE (Name of action)**: The name of the action (e.g., permanent, variable, accidental, seismic) to which the load case belongs. It determines default safety/combination behavior via design-code definitions (via INI-file), and may be extended with an **action category letter A–Z** using an underscore suffix (affecting coefficients/factors).

**2) Stress reference basis**
- **CST (Cross section type for stresses)**: Controls which construction-stage or final section geometry the stored internal forces/moments are interpreted against. It is essential for correct stress calculation.
  - Supported CST values include:
    - **nnnn**: construction stage number
    - **GROS**: gross cross section
    - **CS0 / CS1 / CS255**: construction stage section variants 0, 1, and 255
    - (The documentation also refers to section reference point selection like **STD, PART, EFFE, NULL**, with conversions depending on REF or stored beam geometry; CST/REF together establish where the elastic center is located for stress transformation.)
  - Default: shown as “*”, meaning a program default is applied when omitted. In the surrounding context: default CST is typically **CS1** for all load case types except **G1 and PR (default CS0)**; if CS is undefined, the load case operates on the **gross section**.

- **REF (Reference point of stored forces and moments)**: Determines the reference point for forces/moments that were stored in the database, and thus how they must be interpreted when computing stresses.
  - REF options include:
    - **STD**: current section (no conversion)
    - **GROS**: final gross section
    - **EFFE**: final effective section
    - **PART**: construction stage section
    - **NULL**: original sectional coordinates
  - Default: “PART” is specified.

**3) Labeling**
- **TITI(TIL) / TITL (Name/title of the load case)**: Text label for the load case. It can create a new load case title or modify an existing stored title for later database records. Type is “LIT24”, default “*” (a default/program behavior if unspecified).

**4) Combination and safety factors**
- **GAMU (Unfavourable safety factor)** and **GAMF (Favourable safety factor)**: Factors applied depending on sign/favourability within design checking. Both have default “*”.
- **PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PSIS (Combination coefficients)**:
  - PSI0: standard
  - PSI1: frequent
  - PSI2: quasi-permanent
  - PSIS: infrequent
  These link variable actions to different combinations (rare/frequent/quasi-permanent). All show default “*”.
- **GAMA (Safety factor accidental)**: Additional factor for accidental action checks; default “*”.

**5) Action partitioning and superposition within an action**
- **APAR (Partition of action: G, P, Q, A or E)**: Indicates which action group/category the partition relates to for superposition logic inside a category. Default “*”.
- **SUP (Superposition within action)**: Controls how multiple load cases are superposed under the same action. Default “*”.

**6) Special fatigue amplification**
- **FAT (Special enlargement for fatigue / DIN FB 102 A 106.2)**: A fatigue-related enlargement factor; unit “LIT”, default is “-” (not applied unless specified). The context states FAT enlarges sectional forces by a factor between **1.40 and 1.75** depending on span location rules.

Overall, the table specifies the parameters required to classify a load case by **action type**, map its stored forces/moments to the correct **section reference/elastic center context**, and optionally override or define **safety/combination factors** and special modifiers (fatigue).

content:
The table defines the mapping between three naming/selection fields used for load cases and their typical semantic “Remark” descriptions. It has four columns:

1) **Normal**: the main short code representing a load case type in a “normal” context.  
2) **Add.**: the corresponding short code used when the load case is treated as an additional type.  
3) **Spec.**: the corresponding short code used when the load case is treated as a special type (e.g., within design logic that distinguishes special coefficients/types).  
4) **Remark**: a human-readable interpretation of the load case type.

Across the rows, each “Normal” code is paired with an “Add.” and a “Spec.” code. In other words, the table provides a consistent renaming scheme: whenever a particular load case category is selected under “Normal”, there are corresponding code variants for “Add.” and “Spec.” variants. The base letters typically match the “action” category indicated by the remark (e.g., **G** for dead loads, **Q** for variable loads, etc.), while suffixes/structure reflect the variant type and sometimes the safety/design role.

### Row groups and meanings (from Remark)

**Dead loads / primary dead / secondary dead / prestress / creep-shrinkage (G…)**
- **Gq / ZGq / SGq**: *dead load*  
- **G1g / Z1g / S1q**: *primary dead load*  
- **G2g / Z2g / S2q**: *secondary dead load*  
- **Pg / ZPg / SPq**: *prestress*  
- **Cg / ZCg / SCq**: *creep and shrinkage*  

These indicate that permanent-type actions are expressed with **g** in the Normal codes and map to **Z…** (Add.) and **S…** (Spec.) forms.

**Variable loads and service actions (Q…, Lx…, Wx…, Sq…, Rg…, Fq…, Tx…)**
- **Qq / ZQq / SQq**: *variable load*  
- **Lx / ZLx / SLx**: *life load*  
- **Wx / ZWx / SWx**: *wind* (explicit note: use **ZW** for bridges)  
- **Sq / ZSx / SSx**: *snow* (explicit note: use **ZS** for bridges)  
- **Rg / ZRx / SRx**: *earth pressure, water pressure*  
- **Fq / ZF— / SF—**: *settlements* (*ZF = expected*, *SF = possible*)  
- **Tx / ZTx / STx**: *temperature*  

These rows show that non-permanent variable actions may use the **q/x** suffixes in the Normal code, with parallel **Z…** and **S…** encodings for Add./Spec. Special remarks clarify that for some actions (wind, snow) bridge-specific usage is implied by choosing the **Z…** variant; for settlements, expected/possible are distinguished by **ZF** vs **SF**-like interpretations.

**Accidental and seismic (Ax…, Bx…, Ex…)**
- **Ax / ZAx / SAx**: *accidental*  
- **Bx / ZBx / SBx**: *construction, maintenance*  
- **Ex / ZEx / SEx**: *earthquake* (note: **ZE = Service**, **SE = Design**)  

Thus, earthquake has two roles implied by the “variant”: the **ZE** version corresponds to service-level earthquake and **SE** corresponds to design-level earthquake.

### Practical interpretation for RAG
In the broader system context, this table functions as a **lookup/translation layer** between shorthand type codes used when defining **load cases** (or their categories) and the **typical action meaning**. When a consumer parses a design input, the “Normal/Add./Spec.” code selected determines which coefficient set or design-treatment category is applied, and the corresponding remark provides semantic identification of the action (dead, prestress, creep, wind, snow, settlements, temperature, accidental, construction, earthquake).

 LC is used to select the load cases to be designed. The first item NO may be specified with a number, an expression with wildcard symbol (eg. "‘1??00"’) for load case numbers or the name of a load case type (action). In the latter cases all load cases matching the criteria will be selected. Especially interesting are:
 (D) Ultimate Design combination
 (A) Ultimate Accidental combination
 (E) Ultimate Earthquake combination
 (P) Service: Quasi-permanent combination
 (F) Service: Frequent combination
 (N) Service: Infrequent combination
 (R) Service: Characteristic (rare) combination
 (H) Comb. of principal loading
 (HZ) Comb. of principal+supplemental loading
 (PT) permanent load combination e.g. for timber
 (LT) long term load combination e.g. for timber
 (MT) middle term load combination e.g. for timber
 (ST) short term load combination e.g. for timber
 (VT) very short term load combination e.g. for timber
 The load type is the name of the action to which the load case belongs. The default are the already defined values, but it is possible to redefine all properties temporarily.
 The most important actions are predefined with the INI-file of the design code. Further it is possible to subdivide each action in categories selected with a character from A to Z, each having distinguished combination coefficients or safety factors. This will be appended with an underscore to the name of the action.
 However 48 reserved names with designated meanings are used to trigger special effects in AQB for historical superpositions. AQB saves results in the data base of the design for all combinations (COMB) with an explicit LCST given and for all single load cases with one of the above types assigned. If a load case should be classified only temporarily the type (-) may be used.. Normal Add.. Spec.. Remark. g. Load case is permanent (always added). q. Load case is conditional (added if unfavourable).
 Load cases are conditional excluding each other
 TITL can be used not only to title a load case which is to be newly defined, but can also make a later change or expand the name of a load case which is stored in the database.
 Prestressing is only taken into consideration when a load case with that type of action is se- lected. The factor in the combination will be also applied to the tension force itself if the action does not have a category. With category 0 or 1 these define the factor for pre-tensioning or post-tensioning only. Beside this the factor max not be specified differently, only the first definition is taken.
 When designing individual load cases with prestressing, therefore, all load cases must be given a prestress action type.
 For the check STRE U according the "‘Nachrechnungsrichtline"’ we have reduction factors rcp derived from the shear links provided. They will be applied as additional factors.
 With a definition of FAT DIN the sectional forces of this load case will be magnified based on the location of the section with a factor between 1.40 and 1.75 according to paragraph A 106.2 of DIN FB 102. Unfortunately the information about the start and the end of a span is hardly defined. AQB will use the higher factors therefore only if the beam contains a section with the attribute ”face” towards the respective end of the span.
 The definition of the section type and reference is an essential input to calculate the stresses with the appropriate section.
 Within the static analysis all forces should be referenced to the elastic center of the appropriate construction stage section as caclculated in AQUA. This is the point within a section where an acting normal force will create only centric strains and thus no moments:
 The association of the correct section type can be done either by a global construction stage number or by the section designation defined explictly in the BEAM record. The default for CST is CS1 for all load case types except G1 and PR; for these the default is CS0. Load cases with undefined CS sections are assigned to the gross section. Therefore, when the CS values are not defined in the BEAM record, all load cases operate on the gross section.
