content:
The default for CST is CS1 for all load case types except G1 and PR; for these the default is CS0. Load cases with undefined CS sections are assigned to the gross section. Therefore, when the CS values are not defined in the BEAM record, all load cases operate on the gross section..
 For special cases, the specified sections may be taken to other reference points via REF or via explicit coordinates within the S-record.
 For the calculation of the stresses ideal sections including ducts, tendons and current amount of reinforcements will be used, thus the specified moments will be adjusted then to account for the final shift of the elastic center.
 AQB has various ways of using load cases:
 1. No specification for LC
 If nothing is specified for LC, all load cases stored in the database are designed individu- ally. External forces and moments S are processed separately as load case 0.
 2. Specification for LC only
 When LC is specified, only these load cases are designed.
 3. LC and S
 If internal forces and moments are defined after any LC record, they are saved under this load case and are included in the remaining calculation. This option not only permits the definition of load cases for sections, but also allows the inclusion of additional forces and moments in the calculation for individual sections, even without static design to an existing system. This causes deletion of results stored under the same load case number.
 4. LC and COMB
 If design combinations are selected in addition, then only these combinations are de- signed. The load case types are evaluated only in connection with these combination regulations. The input of COMB supplements the possibilities of the program MAXIMA, and allows calculation with divided safety coefficients, or selection from among traffic load cases.
 The internal forces and moments of the load case, if any, must be input immediately following the LC record. Internal stresses are automatically deleted when internal forces and moments are input.
 The combination coefficients and safety factors will be usually defined with the generation of the load case. A definition in AQB will be only of temporarily influence and will not account for any defaults by specifying a load case type. Only in those cases where forces and moments are defined in AQB explicitly, the defaults from the corresponding INI-file will be taken.
 The items APAR and SUP define the superposition of load cases within an action. The default will be taken from the action. However if only one of the values is specified, the other value will be reset to its default value.

content:
The table defines a set of **internal force and moment quantities** for a structural beam element at specified locations, intended to be used as input for a separate design/analysis of **individual internal forces and moments**. These quantities are associated with a **cross section** and an **element location** along the beam, and they may be stored under different load case rules depending on whether a separate load case identifier is provided (see context: forces/moments defined with *S* are typically saved under load case **0**, while using *LC* stores them under the latest defined load case and requires an explicit section reference coordinate setting).

## Key identification fields
- **NCS (Cross section number)**: selects the cross-section definition used for interpreting the internal forces. Unit: “–”. Default: “–”.
- **NO (Element number)**: identifies which beam element the record belongs to. Unit: “–”. Default: **1**.
- **X (X value)**: the position along the element. Unit: **[m]1001**. Default: **0**.  
  Notes from context: **Negative X** values are interpreted as distances measured from the **beam end** rather than from the start.

## Internal force and moment components
All listed force/moment values are input with the convention described in the context:

- **N (Axial force)**: axial force. Unit: **[kN]1101**. Default **0**.
- **VY (Shear force)**: shear force component in Y direction. Unit: **[kN]1102**. Default **0**.
- **VZ (Shear force)**: shear force component in Z direction. Unit: **[kN]1102**. Default **0**.
- **MT (Total torsional moment)**: total torsional moment (primary torsion + secondary part from warping torsion). Unit: **[kNm]1103**. Default **0**.
- **MY (Bending moment)**: bending moment about Y axis. Unit: **[kNm]1104**. Default **0**.
- **MZ (Bending moment)**: bending moment about Z axis. Unit: **[kNm]1104**. Default **0**.
- **MB (Warping moment)**: warping moment (eigen stress state). Unit: **[kNm²]1105**. Default **0**.
- **MT2 (Secondary torsional moment)**: secondary torsional/warping-related moment component. Unit: **[kNm]1103**. Default **0**.

## Reference coordinates for section offsets
The table includes optional fields that define **where** in the section the moments/shears are referenced:

- **Y (Reference coordinates)**: Y reference coordinate. Unit: **[mm]1011**. Default “*”.
- **Z (Reference coordinates)**: Z reference coordinate. Unit: **[mm]1011**. Default “*”.
- **REF (Designation of a sectional point)**: identifies a particular sectional point reference. Unit type “Lit8”. Default “–”.

Context interpretation:
- By default, **axial force and bending moments** are referenced to the **centroid**, while **torsional moment and shear forces** are referenced to the **centre of shear** of the section.
- If **Y**/**Z** (or an equivalent sectional point **REF**) is specified, then **all internal forces and moments are treated relative to that chosen reference point** in the section coordinate system and are then **transformed** immediately back to the centroid/centre-of-shear reference for internal use.

## Input ordering/uniqueness constraints (from context)
When multiple records are provided, they must be entered in **increasing sequential order by beam number and X value**, and **multiple definitions for the same location are not allowed**. This enables consistent mapping of the defined internal force/moment states along the element.

See also: LC
 S
 These records can be used to define individual internal forces and moments for a separate design.
 The forces and moments defined with S are normally saved under load case number 0. The values NO and X are then needed only for identifying the output.
 If a load case is given with LC, the internal forces and moments are stored under the latest defined load case. In this case the section NCS is used only to define the reference coordinates but must be specified explicitly The forces and moments must be input in increasing sequential order by beam number and x value. Multiple definitions for the same location are not possible. Negative x values are interpreted as dimensions from the beam end.
 Axial force and bending moments are referenced to the centroid, torsional moment and shear- ing forces to the centre of shear of the section. If a specification for Y or Z is made, however, then all internal forces and moments are relative to the so-defined reference point in the section coordinate system. They are immediately transformed to the centroid or the centre of shear. The torsional moment is the total moment as the sum from the primary Saint-Venant and the secondary part from warping torsion. The warping moment MB is an eigen stress state, thus it will not be included in DESI. However for NSTR it will be included as primary strain, but will not varied within a nonlinear analysis.
 Forces and moments for the load case pre- and post tensioning have to be defined always with the static determined part of the prestress forces.
 As the second order analysis must not include the prestressing force in the geometric stiffness, there is an exception: Prestress including creep and shrinkage effects defined with the section (AQUA) is not to be included with the forces and moments if no construction stages have been selected.

The table is a parameter reference for **AQB load-case combinations**, focusing on how to **select the section and the name/identity** used when computing special results—specifically for **EIGE / DESI / NSTR**. Each row defines an “Item” (a keyword), a human-readable “Description,” the “Unit” (if applicable), and a “Default” value.

## Column meanings
- **Item**: the keyword used in input.
- **Description**: what the parameter controls.
- **Unit**: unit expected by the system (blank or shown as a code like `LIT/-` indicates a literal/code list rather than a physical unit).
- **Default**: the default value if the field is not set; often `*` indicates a required/conditional default or that it must be provided depending on context.

## Row 1: `CST` (Section type for EIGE / DESI / NSTR)
- **Purpose**: selects the **section type** used for computations that relate to:
  - **EIGE** – Determination of Internal Stresses (AQBS only)
  - **DESI / NSTR** – non-linear stresses (as referenced in the surrounding context text)
- **Allowed values (enumeration)** shown in the description:
  - **`GROS`**: *Gross section*
  - **`nn`**: *explicit construction stage* (stage number represented as `nn`)
  - **`CS0`**: *Construction stage section 0*
  - **`CS255`**: *Construction stage section 255*
- **Unit column**: `LIT/-` indicates this is a literal or code selector, not a numeric physical quantity.
- **Default**: `*` meaning no meaningful physical default; it must be defined (or is system-determined) for the selected design task. In practice, this parameter governs which geometric/age-related section definition the solver uses when generating internal stress or non-linear stress results.

## Row 2: `TITL` (Name of the combination)
- **Purpose**: provides the **explicit name of the load combination**.
- **Connection to combination behavior** (from the context): if `TITL` is **not selected**, AQB constructs a name automatically from the involved load cases. Therefore, `TITL` overrides the auto-generated naming and fixes the label under which combination results are stored and referenced later.
- **Unit column**: `Lit24` indicates a text/literal field with a specific length/class in the input schema.
- **Default**: `*` meaning it is typically optional, but if omitted, naming will be auto-constructed as described.

Overall, this table defines two key inputs for combination setup: `CST` determines the **section basis** for EIGE/DESI/NSTR calculations, while `TITL` ensures the combination has a **stable, user-defined identifier** (or else AQB generates one automatically).

sections: 3.12 COMB – Definition of Load Case Combinations

content:
The table is a keyword-to-parameter mapping that defines symbolic design variables and their underlying expressions used in load-case combination and/or long-term effects (e.g., creep/shrinkage/relaxation-related internal stress calculations) following common Eurocode-style notation (explicit references to **EN 1990 (Tab. B.3 and eq. 6.10)** appear in the text around the table). It is organized into two columns of paired entries: a **left block** of parameter codes and definitions, and a **right block** of corresponding codes and definitions.

**Left block (GAM / GAMU / PSI… / KFI… / X… codes):**
- **GAM** = \( \gamma_u/\gamma_f \)  
- **GAMU** = \( \gamma_u \)  
- **PSI0** = \( \psi_0 \), **PSI2** = \( \psi_2 \), **PSIG** = \( (\gamma_u/\gamma_f)\cdot \psi_0 \), **PSIU** = \( \gamma_u\cdot \psi_0 \)  
- **PS1G** = \( (\gamma_u/\gamma_f)\cdot \psi_1 \), **PS1U** = \( \gamma_u\cdot \psi_1 \), **PS2G** = \( (\gamma_u/\gamma_f)\cdot \psi_2 \), **PS2U** = \( \gamma_u\cdot \psi_2 \)
- **P1SG** = \( (\gamma_u/\gamma_f)\cdot \psi_{1,inf,q} \), **P1SU** = \( \gamma_u\cdot \psi_{1,inf,q} \)
- **KFI** = \( k_{fi} \)
- **XSIG** = \( \xi\cdot (\gamma_u/\gamma_f) \), **XSIU** = \( \xi\cdot \gamma_u \)
- **KFG** = \( k_{fi}\cdot (\gamma_u/\gamma_f) \)
- **KFG0** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \psi_0 \cdot (\gamma_u/\gamma_f) \)
- **KFG2** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \psi_2 \cdot (\gamma_u/\gamma_f) \)
- **XKFG** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \xi\cdot (\gamma_u/\gamma_f) \)
- **XKGU** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \xi\cdot \gamma_u \)

**Right block (GAMA / GAM E / PS1… / KF… / X… codes):**
- **GAMA** = \( \gamma_a \)
- **GAME** = \( \gamma_f \)
- **PSI1** = \( \psi_1 \), **PS1S** = \( \psi_{1,inf,q} \)  
- **PSIA** = \( \gamma_a\cdot \psi_0 \), **PSIF** = \( \gamma_f\cdot \psi_0 \)  
- **PS1A** = \( \gamma_a\cdot \psi_1 \), **PS1F** = \( \gamma_f\cdot \psi_1 \)  
- **PS2A** = \( \gamma_a\cdot \psi_2 \), **PS2F** = \( \gamma_f\cdot \psi_2 \)  
- **P1SA** = \( \gamma_a\cdot \psi_{1,inf,q} \), **P1SF** = \( \gamma_f\cdot \psi_{1,inf,q} \)
- **XSI** = \( \xi \)
- **X SIF** variants:  
  - **XSIA** = \( \xi\cdot \gamma_a \)  
  - **XSIF** = \( \xi\cdot \gamma_f \)
- **KF** = \( k_{fi} \)
- **XKFI** = \( \xi\cdot k_{fi} \)
- **KFG1** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \psi_1 \cdot \gamma_a/\text{(as shown)}\): explicitly given as \( k_{fi}\cdot \psi_1\cdot \gamma_u/\gamma_f \) is not in this block; instead the right side shows:  
  - **KFG1** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \psi_1\cdot \gamma_u/\gamma_f \) (as transcribed from the table, matching the right-side style)  
- **KFGA** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \xi\cdot \gamma_a \)
- **K FGF** = \( k_{fi}\cdot \xi\cdot \gamma_f \)

**Interpretation of symbols:** across both blocks the codes combine base factors \( \gamma_u \), \( \gamma_f \), \( \gamma_a \) (gamma factors), \( \psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2 \) (psi factors), and \( \psi_{1,inf,q} \) (an “infinite” or long-term psi value under sustained load \(q\)), along with \( k_{fi} \) (a coefficient), and \( \xi \) (a factor multiplying other parameters). Many “G/U” suffixes indicate whether the expression uses \( \gamma_u \) (U) or \( \gamma_u/\gamma_f \) (G) versus “A/F” suffixes indicating \( \gamma_a \) (A) or \( \gamma_f \) (F).

In RAG terms, this table should be stored as a **lookup dictionary**: for each keyword (e.g., `PS1G`, `XSIU`, `KFG0`, `KFGA`) retrieve the exact algebraic definition shown, including multiplication structure and the specific gamma/psi variant used.

The horizontal axis is unlabeled but clearly represents a reference variable (likely time, temperature difference, or another control parameter). The plot includes a baseline horizontal line near the middle, and several curve shapes showing how an additional moment \(M\) varies:

- Two solid/dashed curve families are shown. One set is labeled “DM1” with a curve that begins at the left and dips downward before rising again, forming a U-like profile. Another line labeled “DM2” appears as a higher (less negative) or differently shaped curve over the baseline.
- A third curve (or additional dashed segments) suggests intermediate behavior between DM1 and DM2, consistent with multiple scenarios or parameter variations.
- Near the right side, the curves rise steeply toward the top-right, with the vertical coordinate marked by a “M” bracket/axis indicator.
- The difference between DM1 and DM2 is visually represented by the separation of their curves: DM2 lies above DM1 for the negative/valley portion, and the curves converge toward the rightmost high moment region.

At the bottom of the image, a caption reads:  
“Figure 3.2: Additional moments for control of cracking”

Overall, the figure is intended to illustrate how “additional moments” (DM1 and DM2) are applied for cracking control, showing their different magnitudes and curve progression across the plotted parameter range.

content:
See also: LC
 AQBS normally performs its design operations for the selected load cases. With COMB, com- binations of the load cases can be defined instead, as are used in partial safety theory in many international codes or prestressed concrete.
 Compared to the superposition in MAXIMA, we need to know the part of the permanent loading, the prestress or the life load for many design tasks. Furthermore it is very common that we have extreme values for different targets, thus the load cases of the same type ar now mutually exclusive.
 The combinations must be input before the particular design request is specified, and will stay in effect for later operations as well, until a new definition is made.
 For each combination you may define a load case number LCST to store results. Then the results are stored under this load case number. These are:
 • Combined forces and moments (not at EIGE) (incl. all special effects and transformations)
 • Stresses for each material and selected stress points or the centre of every shear cut for STRE. For shear stress in concrete we store for the reference stress the shear stress due to lateral shear stress only.
 • Eigenstresses in case of EIGE
 non-linear stresses for DESI and NSTR
 •
 You may also define for every block of combinations two special load case numbers via the combinations GMAX and GMIN with LCST. Then the maximum and minimum values of the results will be stored via this load case numbers in the same format.
 If TITL is not selected, AQB constructs a name of its own from the involved load cases.
 For each load case a number can be specified; then the load case which is addressed thereby is added up without regard for its type. As an alternative, a load type can also be addressed (see record type LC); then all load cases of this type are addressed and combined as selected within the action definition. e.g:
 • For the types G1, G2, P and C, all of the contributing components are added together (permanent loads). Load type G includes all of the G1 and G2 load types.

 For Bridges EN 1992-2 defines in section B.105 safety factors for delayed long term strains to be used, "‘However, when safety would be increased by overestimation of delayed strains, and when it is relevant in the project, the creep and shrinkage predicted on the basis of the formulas or experimental determinations should be multiplied by a safety factor."’ Thus the user has to select these factors via a definition of CTRL EIGE SAFE. The provisions of the German NA to apply these factors always for the shrinkage is activated automatically if a bridge class has been selected.
 If T is defined, these basic values PHI and EPS will be modified according to the evolution in time given by tables or formulas in the design codes. For those design codes relying on the summation approach (DIN 4227, Japanese and Chinese Code) the delayed elasticity will be incorporated automatically. If one wants to apply the time evolution function to be applied to the explicit given PHI/EPS-values, one has to use a negative value for T. For the first creep interval, the value T0 will control the age for the concrete for creeping and the amount of shrinkage which has been occurred between TS and T0. If we need the total shrinkage (e.g. for deformations or stresses with reinforcements) a separate unloaded shrinking time interval has to be introduced.
 The value of TEMP defines then either the temperature in Celsius (1 to 80 degree) during the creep step or, if defined negative the temperature of a thermal treatment before the creep step. For special cases a definition with an explict unit − allows to specify an explicit scaling factor for the effective age of the concrete.
 The influence of the temperature on the tendon relaxation (EN 1992-1-1, 10.3.2.) should be accounted for with an explicit Factor for PHI. The formula (10.2) given in EN 1992-1-1 is not implemented as it yields for Tmax equal to 80 degrees a rapid (43.3 times accelerated) re- laxation, so the method given in many technical papers to apply an immediate loss of 4% is preferable. For very special cases a definition with increased time increment values according to that formula can be specified.

For very special cases a definition with increased time increment values according to that formula can be specified..
 For analysis SUM with delayed elasticity (old DIN and Japan and China) the parts from delayed elasticity are always added if T is specified and applied for all primary creep results with the corresponding negative value. The order of the load numbers must correspond to the chrono- logical course in this case. Higher load case numbers must describe therefore later creep stages. If the PHI value is given as 0.0, the part from delayed elasticity is suppressed. If one wishes to determine only the re-creep, a small value must be entered at PHI.
 Further it has to be taken care of, that the effective concrete age is based on the slowly harden- ing cement, instead of the new coefficients (kz = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5), the original factors from Rüsch (kz = 1.0, 2.0, 3.0) have to be used.
 If an Indian design code is selected, than RH will be treated as maturity according to table 2 of IRC 18 defining PHI, while EPS is derived from the time T0 according to table 3. There are no time effects available however in this case.
 AS 3600 / 5100 provide curves and final factors for creep and shrinkage based on the effective
 depth, the environmental conditions and the concrete strength. Not included are temperature, cements with other sulphate contents or high stresses. With a definition of EC at PHI a switch to the Eurocode-Formulas may be achieved.
 With the setting CTRL EIGE 1, curvature loads for calculating the statically indeterminate shares from creep and shrinkage are stored. As a rule, multiple creep stages are required in that case (e.g. 3 to 5) because STAR2/ASE do not know the stresses or the forces at the end of an interval. If necessary, the relaxation parameters can be altered in AQB. If this load case is not calculated with STAR2/ASE, the calculation for AQB remains unrestrained i.e. statically determined.

content:
The table defines input items for a structural stress/utilisation check (record family STRE). Each row specifies (1) an item keyword, (2) what the value represents, (3) its unit, and (4) a default value or default linkage to another item.

**SMOD (Type of check / material number)**  
- **Default: `E`**  
- Accepts a literal indicating the calculation type or a material identifier for tailoring permissible stresses.  
  - `E`: elastic stresses (used to define sectional classes)  
  - `B`: resistance for forces (utilisation based on force capacity)  
  - `C`: resistance of cross sections (utilisation based on sectional resistance)  
  - `D`: suggested dimensions (dimensioning from allowable/plastic capacities)  
  - `DG`: select a section from a grouped sequence (used when geometry sizing must follow predefined families).  
Context: in all modes, elastic stresses are evaluated first to assign a sectional class. For **class 3**, allowable stresses are checked and the resulting utilisation is stored. For **class 1/2**, resistance per individual force is computed; for `P` the utilisations are linearly summed, while option `C` stores a code-based complex interaction (Eurocode references given).

**STYP (Tabulated limiting stresses)**  
- **Unit: `LIT`**, **Default: `-`** (no numeric default shown)  
- Selects a set of pre-tabulated permissible stresses. Context indicates `STYP` may be a literal that presets safety factors, permissible stresses, and code-specific features, reducing the need for manual limiting stress input.

**SC, ST, SBC, SBT, SBBT / SBBT-like entries (Normal stress limits by location and sign)**  
All have **unit N/mm²** and are used as maxima of specific stress components:  
- `SC`: max normal compressive stress (**Default: `SC`**)  
- `ST`: max normal tensile stress (**Default: `SC`**)  
- `SBC`: max edge bending compression (**Default: `SC`**)  
- `SBT`: max edge bending tension (**Default: `ST`**)  
- `S BBC`: max corner bending compression (**Default: `SBC`**)  
- `SBBC` / `SBBT`: max corner bending tension (**Default: `SBT`**)  
These parameters define the allowable stress ceilings for different cross-section regions (general, edge, corner) and stress types (compression/tension, normal/bending).

**SI, SII (Principal stress limits)**  
- `SI`: max principal tensile stress, **unit N/mm²**, default `-`  
- `SII`: max principal compressive stress, **unit N/mm²**, default `-`  
These define allowable extrema in principal directions.

**TAU, SV, TAUS, SSTM, SSEM, SSKM, SSER, SSKR (Shear and combined stress limits)**  
All are **unit N/mm²** with defaults depending on relation to shear/torsion criteria:  
- `TAU`: max shear stress (Default `-`)  
- `SV`: max equivalent stress (Default `-`)  
- `TAUS`: max shear stress longit. in welds (Default `-`)  
- `SSTM`: max shear/tension torsion middle area (Default: `TAU`)  
- `SSEM`: max shear/tension separate middle area (Default: `TAU`)  
- `SSKM`: max shear/tension combined middle area (Default: `TAU`)  
- `SSER`: max shear/tension edge (Default: `TAU`)  
- `SSKR`: max shear/tension combined edge (Default: `TAU`)  
These items parameterize different shear/combined-stress evaluations across member regions (middle vs edge; separate vs combined) and weld-related directions.

**CC, CBC, CBBC (Compressive zone stress limits)**  
- `CC`: max normal compressive zone stress (**Default: `(SC)`**)  
- `CBC`: max edge compressive zone stress (**Default: `(CC)`**)  
- `CBBC`: max corner compressive zone stress (**Default: `(CBC)`**)  
All in **N/mm²**. They represent allowable compressive stresses for zones, likely used in sectional class 3 checks.

**LIMA, ZMAX, ZDIF (Prestressing-related limits)**  
- `LIMA`: limit for decompression or zone a/b, **N/mm²**, default `*`  
- `ZMAX`: max prestressing steel stress, **N/mm²**, default `*`  
- `ZDIF`: max stress range for prestressing steel, **N/mm²**, default `-`  
The `*` indicates defaults depend on other settings/codes rather than being fixed numeric values.

**SCMG (Global safety class factor)**  
- **Unit: `-`**, no default shown  
- Used to multiply the selected safety factors globally (context: additional factor applied to safety factors).

Overall, the table is a specification of how the analysis software obtains limiting stresses for stress checks and utilisation storage. Values can be either directly provided (by maximum stress limits) or indirectly selected through `SMOD` and `STYP`, with regional mappings (general/edge/corner; normal/bending; principal/shear/combined; compressive zone) and optional prestressing and global safety adjustments.

content:
STRE
 Evaluation of maximum stresses for every force principal and von Mises yield stress in all sectional points.
 E:
 B: Evaluation of the utilisation factors for every individual component and a simplified linear superposition of the linear total utilisation.
 C: Evaluation of the utilisation factors for every individual component and a complex interaction of these components.
 In all cases the elastic stress will be evaluated, as this is required to define a sectional class. If the section is in class 3, the allowable stresses will be checked and their utilisation is save to the data base as relevant utilisation. If the section is in class 1 or 2, the resistance of the cross section for any individual force is calculated and for option P a simple linear addition of all utilization degrees will be saved to the database as total utilisation, while option C will store a complex interaction based on the provisions of the Eurocode (1993/1999).
 Additional tables for every section if ECHO TABS has been set which is also the default value. Loadcases with the extreme values of stresses or utilisation factors may be created in the data base by a preceding COMB GMAX/GMIN. If stress points have been defined in the cross- section, then the stress ranges occurring in the points are saved in the load case specified for GMAX. The stress ranges result from the difference between the maximum and minimum occurring stresses in the analysed load cases or combinations.
 D: Suggested dimensions
 Depending on the section class an estimate for the required dimensions of the cross section is made based on allowable stresses or plastic sectional capacities. For rectangle, circle, and steel shapes a rather detailed analysis is performed, while for all other sections, a linear scaling factor for the dimensions factor is evaluated. In the cases of rectangular sections, the width or height can be fixed when defining the section. Option DE will use only the allowable stresses for the dimensioning.
 Similar to option D. However sections will be selected from a group of sections. A group is defined via a sequence of cross section with continuous section numbers and increasing load capacities. The first section of a group will differ only in the last digit of the current section number. If sections with numbers 8,9,10,11 and 12 are defined, then the program may select instead of section 8 and 9 any of these numbers while for sections 10, 11 and 12 only the last three sections will be used. This Option is especially useful if one wants to select a different sequence for British or American shapes (e.g. UC 305 x 305 x 97 before UC 254 x 254 x 132). Option DGE will use only the allowable stresses for the dimensioning.

Some design codes allow a design for shear of concrete sections based in an uncracked model. These are the old German DIN 4227 or the first amendment to the German "‘Nachrech-
 nungsrichtlinie"’ of the German Ministry of Transport (2015). In all cases the stress at the extreme fiber of the section is not allowed to exceed a certain value.
 For the latter the definition of STRE U has to be selected. Controls the scope where a “constant reinforcement” pattern is applied. Possible settings:

- **GLOB**: in all active beams
- **TOTL**: in all beams

Defines how the last-defined **LCR** case is used and how reinforcement is combined:

- **SING**: single calculation
- **SAVE**: save as global minimum reinforcement
- **SUPE**: superposition with global minimum reinforcement  
- **NEW**: new definition (special cases only)  
Default for **RMOD = SING** (LIT enum). Unit again shown as **LIT**.

The table lists input parameters for a structural cross‑section “stiffness evaluation / checking” workflow (notably for concrete members with reinforcement and possible cracked or nonlinear behavior). ## Core selection: load condition and stiffness evaluation
- **KMOD (Load condition and stiffness evaluation)**: Determines how stresses/stiffness are evaluated for the chosen limit state(s) and analysis mode.
  - Options shown in the description:
    - **SERV**: Stress evaluation without stiffness change.
    - **ULTI**: Change stiffness for this selected condition.
    - **ACCI**: Accidental combination (stiffness settings follow the accidental defaults).
    - **NONL**: Enables non-linear options (also linked to “byproducts” such as stress ranges, crack widths, and non-linear stiffnesses for later use in STAR2/ASE or DYNA).
  - **Default**: “!” indicates a required/mandatory selection (no meaningful default provided).

## Stiffness controls (materials and reinforcement/tension stiffening)
- **KSV (Control for material of the cross section)**: Stiffness control for concrete/material response.
  - **Default**: “*” (set automatically based on KMOD / DESI / NSTR uniqueness).
- **KSB (for reinforcements and tension stiffening)**: Stiffness control governing reinforcement and tension stiffening effects.
  - **Default**: “*” (also auto-derived).
- **KMIN / KMAX (Minimum / Maximum stiffness)**: Numerical bounds on stiffness.
  - **Default**: KMIN = **0.01**, KMAX = **4.00** (unitless stiffness scaling).
- **ALPH (Numerical damping factor)**: Damping for numerical stability.
  - **Default**: **0.4**.
- **FMAX (Numerical acceleration factor)**:
  - **Default**: **5.0**.

### How KSV/KSB defaults are determined (context from remarks)
The defaults depend on **load condition** derived from KMOD (and described as being selected via DESI and NSTR):
- Linear elastic variants:
  - **EL**: linear elastic, but without tension in concrete

  - **SL**: nominal serviceability without safety factor
  - **SLD**: serviceability design with safety factor
  - **UL**: ultimate nominal without safety factor
  - **ULD**: ultimate design with safety factor

 For the design you have to select a crack width. The calculation of the crack width is done for the completed crack pattern according to equation 8.128. The input value BB is used for an explicit parameter ϕ1, default is 1.4.
 This Spanish design code is rather similar to the Eurocode (BB is factor k2). It classifies four possible crack width values (0.40, 0.30, 0.20 and 0.10 mm). But then then formulas for the effective height and the crack distance and the mean strain quite different. Thus there is no dependency on the bond properties of the reinforcements. The distance of the longitudinal
 bars is always taken as 15 ∅, because we have not enough information available for more details. Tension stiffening is treated as with EC 2.
 The check of the decompression for the cracked section is controlled by the definition of NSTR SERV CRAC DECO CW hh, where hh at item CW is the distance to the ducts outer perimeter. The default value for hh is 100 mm, but the INI-file may contain a formula. The strain in these critical points will be printed and saved to the database.

Calculation of non-linear stiffnesses in AQB with other values than S0 is successful only if another program like ASE, STAR2 or DYNA is called again with a new iteration as a restart, and this process is repeated until convergence occurs. Thus it is recommended to define these records within ASE or STAR2 and to define the number of iterations there. Within the procedure WPS/SPS it is possible to call several programs in turn with the option PROG ITER which is optimized however for the use with STAR2 (cf. AQB 5.2.2. prefabricated column).
 An analysis of unloading or the hysteresis of load cycles is not possible today for beam ele- ments!
 Selection of the optimum iteration method is not easy, because the selected type of stiffness update determines the iteration and convergence behaviour. In most cases the use of KMOD S1 or SN will be straight forward. KMOD SN is the fastest method for slightly nonlinear prob- lems, while S1 is suited for highly loaded systems where it may happen that the ultimate load capacity of a section is exceeded within an iteration step. For the methods K0, K1 or KN the stiffness will be kept constant, but plastic strains are calculated, to be used as extra loading as initial strains similar to a temperature loading. Using this approach the failure of the system is no longer given by an instability detected during the solution of the equation system, but by monotone increasing deformations, which have to be checked carefully therefore.
 The user should start with SN for lightly loaded systems and with S1 for more heavily loaded systems, and should then shift to K1 or K0 if necessary. When there are many similar systems, it pays to find the optimum method by experimentation.
 To prevent endangering the iteration procedure, only changes of stiffness of a certain magni- tude are permitted. A value of 0.4 for ALPH means that in each step the stiffness can decrease at most to 0.4 times its last value, or increase at most to 1/0.4 times its last value. ALPH is preset to 0.4 in ASE / STAR2, but to 0.01 in AQB itself. Independently of that, the stiffnesses remain limited to the range between KMIN and KMAX, referenced to the elastic stiffness.

A value of 0.4 for ALPH means that in each step the stiffness can decrease at most to 0.4 times its last value, or increase at most to 1/0.4 times its last value. ALPH is preset to 0.4 in ASE / STAR2, but to 0.01 in AQB itself. Independently of that, the stiffnesses remain limited to the range between KMIN and KMAX, referenced to the elastic stiffness..
 With critical systems, which exceed their loading capacity in the course of the iteration, it may be necessary to limit the maximum acceleration factor with FMAX. A value of less than 1.0 damps the iteration procedure. A value of 0.0 turns the procedure off. The default of FMAX is 2.0 at a calculation with NSTR KMOD SN and CTRL INTE 4.

For coupling joints and other constructions it may be required to design for fatigue with a given stress range. This can be easily accounted for by defining several load cases for the same section. If the fatigue check needs also the permanent stress, you should include one load
 case of type MAXP in the analysis. To save the stress range in the database an extra load case number is required to be specified via COMB GMAX LCST ...
 AQB will keep track of maximum and minimum stresses and will compare the resulting differ- ence with the threshold values specified for concrete and reinforcing steel in AQUA. So gener- ally the allowed stress range should be specified at the material definition. For the simplified check acc. EN 1992-1-1 6.8.6 it is also possible to explicitly set an allowed stress range (e.g. 70 MPa) with the option SIGS. This value is effective for all reinforcement materials. However such a global definition will deactivate some specific stress modifications of the design codes.
 Unless a definition of CTRL REIN FIX/FIXL has been specified, AQB will increase the area of passive reinforcements accordingly, if the limit value for the reinforcements is exceeded. But there will be no reanalysis of the load cases with the changed values. All printed results are therefore valid for the reinforcement before the analysis. Special notice should be given to the fact, that without a preliminary design only the minimum reinforcements for longitudinal and shear links are used.
 For the fatigue design check according to DIN 1045-1 resp. DIN FB-102 the Literal FAT DINF should be entered, further definitions might be done with records LC and BEAM or within the material definition (AQUA).
 It might be helpful to increase the volume of print out via ECHO NSTR EXTR in such cases.

The table defines the **input parameters used to generate sectional capacity results** (either single values or capacity diagrams) for a structural cross-section. It is organized as a compact parameter matrix where each row corresponds to a specific **load case / action type** and each column corresponds to a **capacity evaluation type**, with additional support for defining loads via **forces, moments, strain-based definitions, and reinforcement modifiers**.

### Core columns and meanings
- **CAPA (capacity selection / evaluation mode)**: Sets how the sectional response is evaluated. It includes different limit-state and safety-factor formulations.
- **Item / Description** and **NCS Cross section number (CS)**: Links results to a specific cross-section definition through an NCS cross section number and CS construction stage.
- **TASK**: Selects the computational task to perform.
- **STR (strain evaluation selector)**: Enables evaluation of strains for given actions/loads.
- **DESI (design requirement of reinforcement)**: Computes the required reinforcement for given criteria.
- **Evaluation types (STR / DESI variants, with interaction types)**: The table distinguishes between:
  - **NS / NMS / NM / NMS / NM2 / NMS2 / NM + shear interactions**
  - Examples include **N, NM, NM2**, and **NMS / NMS2** indicating whether normal force–moment interaction and/or normal force–moment–shear interaction are considered, and whether **alternating moment** conditions are enabled.
- **Limit-state / factorization mode** (explicitly listed):  
  - **NONE**: no factorisation (characteristic values)  
  - **SERV**: ultimate limit state for unfactored loads (for some design codes only)  
  - **ULTI**: ultimate limit state  
  - **ACCI**: accidental limit state  
  - **EL/ELD**: elastic characteristic/design  
  - **SL/SLD**: service characteristic/design  
  - **UL/ULD**: ultimate characteristic/design  
  - **CALC/CALD**: calculatoric characteristic/design  
  - **PL/PLD**, **PLB/PLBD**: plastic / stress-block based characteristics  
  These modes control which safety factors and material/behavior assumptions are applied.

### Load input definitions
The table provides a structured way to define sectional effects, using either **forces/moments** directly or **strain/curvature** indirectly:
- **N** / **VY** / **VZ**: Axial force and shear force components, associated with **axial or shear strains** when used in strain-based workflows.
- **MT**: Total torsional moment (or torsional strain).
- **MY / MZ**: Bending moment about axes (or curvature-based definitions).
- **Unit handling**:
  - Forces/moments may be given as **true values** in **[kN]/[kNm]** or as **factors [-]** applied on the single-value capacity.
  - Strains may be specified explicitly with unit **[‰] (o/oo)**.
  - **Curvatures** must be defined as **difference of strains across the section height**.
- **Distortions** are referenced via **GEO_LENGTH[1001]** (geometry-related unit for distortion).

### Reinforcement specification
Reinforcements can be defined in two ways:
1. **Explicit reinforcement areas** in **[cm²]**
2. **As factors [-]** applied to the reinforcement values already defined for the section.

### Example of numeric capacity columns (visible rows)
The shown numeric entries correspond to target capacity parameters (e.g., **LT**, **STR**, **UL** and **ULTI** scenarios) with identifiers:
- **[kN]1101** and **[kN]1102** (axial force capacities or thresholds)
- **[kNm]1103 / [kNm]1104** (bending moment capacities)
- **[kNm²]1105** (torsional/interaction moment-squared style capacity measure)
All visible values are currently **0**, indicating placeholders for input or computed results depending on the selected task and capacity mode.

Overall, this table is a configuration layer that connects **cross-section metadata**, **evaluation method (TASK/STR/DESI)**, **limit state selection**, and **action definition (forces/moments vs strains/curvatures)** to enable automated generation of **sectional capacity outputs** and diagrams.

The input table defines the **section capacity “case” parameters** used by the calculator to generate **single values and sectional diagrams** of torsional and (optionally) reinforcement-dependent capacities. It is structured with four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

### Item column (parameter identifiers)
The table lists parameter codes that control what the sectional analysis computes and how reinforcement is represented.

### Parameter groups and meanings
1. **MT2 — 2ndary torsional moment**
   - **Description:** “2ndary torsional moment”
   - **Unit:** **[kNm]**
   - **Unit code shown:** **1103**
   - **Default:** **0**
   - **Role in analysis:** MT2 allows the model to include an additional torsional component (“secondary torsion”) in the section response evaluation.

2. **AS0 … AS9 — Reinforcements of layer 0 to 9**
   - **Descriptions:**
     - **AS0:** Reinforcements of layer 0  
     - **AS1:** Reinforcements of layer 1  
     - …  
     - **AS9:** Reinforcements of layer 9
   - **Unit:** **[cm²]**
   - **Unit code shown:** **1020**
   - **Default:** shown as **\*** (asterisk)
   - **Role in analysis:** These entries specify reinforcement areas **per discrete reinforcement layer** (0 through 9). Each layer’s reinforcement can be set explicitly in **cm²** or (per the surrounding context) can also be interpreted as **factors [-]** relative to reinforcement values defined in the section model. The asterisk default typically indicates “use section-defined default” or “parameter is optional/overridable” rather than a fixed numeric default.

3. **CMNT — Short comment**
   - **Description:** “Short comment”
   - **Unit:** **[ ]Lit16** (a literal/text field unit)
   - **Default:** **\***
   - **Role in analysis:** Provides a freeform short textual annotation associated with the capacity record/case for documentation purposes.

### Overall behavior and output linkage (context from provided text)
These records are designed to create sectional capacity results under varying **force/moment/strain states**. The broader configuration text indicates that loads can be entered either as **true values** or as **factors** applied to characteristic capacities, and that torsion/moments/forces may be combined with reinforcement inputs. Curvatures and distortions have specialized input conventions (curvatures from strain differences; distortions via a GEO_LENGTH reference). Reinforcement layers (AS0–AS9) are therefore key inputs to the capacity evaluation, enabling generation of reinforcement-dependent capacity values and diagrams.

In summary, the table primarily parameterizes **secondary torsion (MT2)** and **distributed reinforcement layers (AS0–AS9)**, with an optional **comment (CMNT)**, supporting the construction of sectional capacity results in the associated calculator workflow.

 These records allow to create single values or diagrams of sectional capacities.
 Forces and moments may be defined as true values, as factors [-] on the single value capac- ity. Alternatively strains with the explicit unit [o/oo] may be defined. Curvatures have to be defined as difference of strains across the section height. Distortions are refered to the unit GEO_LENGTH[1001].
 Reinforcements may be specified explicitly in [cm2] or as factors [-] on the values defined in the section.

All forces will be converted to corresponding elastic strains. Then the non linear normal and shear stresses will be evaluated based on the superposition of all strains and integrated to total forces and moments.

The task STR will be evaluated for a set of strains and presented graphically. The curvatures ky and kz will be scaled simultaneously from 0 to the maximum value of MY and MZ. All other strains will be unchanged. However, if N is defined as force, an iteration of the central strain will be done, to match these normal force. (See S1/K1 in record NSTR).
 The maximum strains will be controlled if any design state is selected, and exceedence of the limit strains will be flagged.

The task STR will be evaluated for a set of limit strains and presented graphically. The central strain and the curvatures will be selected based on the design code limit strains and the ratio of ky and kz. All other strains will be unchanged. However, if MY and MZ are given as forces and biaxial bending ist active, an iteration of the orientation of the neutral axis will be performed to give a planar meridian cut of the interaction surface.

The table is a configuration/parameter description for an output control block used to print or omit different analysis/design result sections in a structural engineering program. It contains four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

### Columns
- **Item**: Names the field being configured in a record (e.g., `OPT`, `VAL`, `SELE`).
- **Description**: Explains the allowed values and their meaning.
- **Unit**: Mostly shows a constant/placeholder value (e.g., `LIT`), indicating the field is a symbolic selector rather than a physical quantity.
- **Default**: The default value used if the option is not specified.

### Field: `OPT` (Output option selector)
`OPT` specifies which group of results (a functional output module) should be controlled. The default for `OPT` is **FULL**, meaning that, unless changed by `VAL`, all options in this group (except special exclusions noted elsewhere) are enabled.

Allowed `OPT` values in the table include:
- `SECT` – Static properties of section  
- `FORC` – Forces and moments  
- `COMB` – Combinations and their forces  
- `STRE` – Elastic stresses  
- `DESI` – Design  
- `NSTR` – Non-linear stresses  
- `EIGe` – Finding internal stresses (spelled as `EIGE` in the context text)  
- `SHEA` – Shear design  
- `CRAC` – Limitation of crack width  
- `FAT` – Fatigue design  
- `C2T` – c/t slenderness ratio  
- `USEP` – Used participle factors  
- `REIN` – Reinforcements  
- `TABS` – Tabular summaries  
- `SSUM` – Maximum forces and moments  
- `LC` – Individual load cases  
- `BSEC` – Sections  
- `STAT` – Overview of CPU time  
Additionally, `FULL` is described as **All options except for LC, BSEC**.

In other words, `OPT` determines *what kind* of results you are configuring.

### Field: `VAL` (Output intensity / printing behavior)
`VAL` controls how much information is produced for the selected `OPT`. The default is **FULL**.

Allowed `VAL` values:
- `OFF` – nothing computed / printed  
- `NO` – no output  
- `YES` – standard output (default in general)  
- `FULL` – full output  
- `EXTR` – extended output (more detailed; may split across several tables)

This means `VAL` determines *how much* of the chosen result content is emitted.

### Field: `SELE` (Selection mask)
The table footer introduces `SELE` as an **Output mask** (with default `LIT4` / `*` shown in the screenshot). While the screenshot does not list all mask semantics, the surrounding context text clarifies that many `ECHO <module>` and related settings can act as output toggles and masks for stresses, load cases, stress points/elements, reinforcement states, etc.

### Overall interpretation
Together, the table defines a two-level output control mechanism:
1) **Choose result module(s)** with `OPT` (e.g., `FORC`, `STRE`, `C2T`, `REIN`).
2) **Choose output depth** with `VAL` (from `OFF/NO` up to `FULL/EXTR`).
A selection mask (`SELE`) can further refine which sub-items (e.g., stress points, stress components, load cases, or tendon groups) are printed.

All elements (parts) of a cross section are marked from program AQUA with a literal with up to 4 characters. The output of selected values (polygon points, reinforcement etc.) contains only the elements which match any defined mask SELE. Multiple SELE definitions for every option are possible.
 SELE is a literal with up to 4 characters which may contain wildcard-symbols. These are:
 ’*’ for any number of any characters
 ’?’ for any character
 for example the literal
 ’A*’ includes all words who start with A
 ’?0’ includes all words with two characters with second character ’0’
 ’1??0’ includes all words with 4 characters with first character ’1’ and last character ’0’
 ’*’ can be any word
 or any other with any character after ’*’ are equivalent to the literal up to ’*’.
